speechtext:
Hon. H. A. STEWART (Minister of public Works) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to authorize the Minister of Public Works, on behalf of His Majesty, to enter into an agreement with the corporation of the city of Ottawa to extend the period of the existing agreement with the corporation for one year from July 1, 1934,
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Smith (Cumberland) in the chair.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT
speechtext:
The object of this resolution is to authorize the continuance of an agreement between the Dominion of Canada and the city of Ottawa for a further period of one year. The matter has been before the house on other occasions during the
City of Ottawa Agreement

last three or four years, and it simply continues the existing agreement under which $100,000 is paid for water supplied by the city of Ottawa for fire protection in connection with the parliament buildings. The water which is supplied to the buildings used as offices is paid for on a meter basis, and the agreement also contains certain provisions with respect to the maintenance of streets, pavements and bridges. This continues the existing arrangement for another year.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT
speechtext: How long has the present agreement been in force?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT
speechtext: The agreement was made in 1924 for one year, to July, 1925, and then it was extended for five years from July, 1925, to 1930, and the amount was increased from $75,000 to $100,000 per annum. It has been extended annually since that time on the basis of $100,000 -per annum.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT
speechtext: Has there 'been any change either in the amount or in the terms since 1930?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT
speechtext: No.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT
speechtext: Were any representations made this year by the mayor or the city officials with regard to increasing the grant?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT
speechtext: I do not think any representations have been made in connection with an increase in the amount desired for this service. There were representations in connection with other matters in which the city of Ottawa is interested but which are outside the scope of this agreement entirely. There was some suggestion that the amount paid was not all it should be, but it never took the form of any definite negotiations.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT
speechtext: I take it from what the minister says that it was never pointed out that, while the government property cannot be taxed, neverthless the total assessment has been made by the assessment commissioner of Ottawa. Can the minister tell us what that amounts to?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT
speechtext: I have not that information before me. The property of course is by statute exempt from taxation. I believe they do carry on their assessment rolls a valuation, but the procedure is an innocuous one, because there is no power to assess.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT
speechtext:
I know. I will be glad to tell the minister what the amount of assessment is on the rolls. I admit the property
cannot be taxed, but nevertheless the assessment commissioner of Ottawa each year places

the assessment on the rolls. The value is $40,907,484. If this were taxed at the general public school rate of city taxation, the tax would amount to $1,505,394.41 per annum. I got that information from the city officials.
I merely want to point out to the minister that we are not over-generous to the city of Ottawa and that the grant is pretty low.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT
speechtext: This is rather a big subject, and as I have said, it is outside the scope of this agreement. I would like to ask my hon. friend whether the -total assessment of $40,000,000 includes all the buildings that are occupied by the government and for which they pay rent.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT
speechtext: I understand this is on government owned property in the city of Ottawa. I may be mistaken, but that was my information.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT
speechtext: Of course, as my hon. friend knows, in respect of buildings which the government rents-and there is a large number of them and the rental paid is very large-they are not exempt from taxation; we pay taxes either in rental or specifically.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT
speechtext: Does the minister think this represents a very fair bargain on the part of the government for what the city does?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT
speechtext: It is an agreement made some years ago. As I have pointed out, for all the offices where water is supplied we pay on meter the regular city rate. This is only for water for fire protection and for the parks. Whether it be fair or not is a very big question and it cannot be determined exactly by itself, because it is linked up with other matters such as grants to the federal district commission and other features that are taken into consideration. I would not like to say whether the amount is too much or too little, but I think it is fairly reasonable. It is based on an agreement anyway and shows an increase of $25,000 per annum over the amount that was agreed upon previously. I think it is fairly reasonable, but all these matters are, as I say, more or less connected and will have to be considered together.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT
speechtext: Has the city of Ottawa expressed its approval of this proposition?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT
speechtext: The city of Ottaw-a would perhaps like to get a larger amount, but unless a bill founded on this resolution is passed there will not be any authority for paying any amount.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Could the minister state how the amount of $100,000 was arrived at?

City of Ottawa Agreement

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT
speechtext: By negotiation and agreement between the city and the government. As I said, prior to 1925 the amount was $75,000 and it was then increased to $100,000, the amount that has been paid since.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT
speechtext: The mere recital of figures does not convey very much meaning to me. I would like to know what value the government obtains in return for this expenditure of $100,000 per annum.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT
speechtext: We get water for fire protection and for services in the parks.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT
speechtext: What is actually the amount of water used in the parks?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT
speechtext: There is no meter, I believe, for that. The meter is on the buildings and offices, but I do not think there is any meter on the quantity that goes this other way.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT
speechtext: I would have preferred it had the minister given to the committee some method by which the amount of $100,000 could be computed, so that we could vote on the matter more intelligently. I do not know whether the amount is too large or too small. Naturally I can understand hon. members representing Ottawa constituencies trying to obtain from the government as good a measure of support for the city as they possibly can; on the other hand, those who do not come from Ottawa would like to have some idea of the equity of the amount arrived at as between the city and the central authority. At the present time, w'hile I certainly cannot object to the amount, neither can I approve it because in what the minister has said there is nothing to give me an intelligent idea as to how to vote on this particular question.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT
speechtext:
I am sorry I
cannot give the hon. member the information because the agreement was negotiated before I had anything to do with this matter. All I can say is that it is the result of negotiation embodied in an agreement. It must have been considered fair at the time the agreement was made.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT
speechtext:
On the face of it, it seems
a rather large sum of money to pay for the services rendered. I may be wrong in my understanding of the matter and as I say, I would be able to understand the matter better if we had the agreement before the committee; we would then know a little more about the matter than we do at present.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Do I understand from
the minister that the government pays 8100,000 a year merely for watering the lawn in front of the parliament buildings?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT
speechtext: No, that is for fire protection and parks all through the city. The park system is under the control of the federal district commission; it is rather extensive.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT
speechtext:
We have heard the Ottawa
representatives complaining about the amount. There are civic parks in all parts of the dominion and the local authorities are compelled to pay for their own water. Evidently the federal authorities are providing Ottawa with parks at federal expense and in addition we have to provide and pay for the water which we use in the beautification of those parks for the benefit of the people of this city. We have, I suppose, other similar expenditures to consider and I certainly would like to have if possible a little more information from the minister in regard to the equity of this agreement.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT
speechtext:
I think the
treatment of the city is fairly generous. I do not know how the members representing the city of Ottawa will take that remark, but when all that is being done by the government in every direction, of which this is only a very small item, is considered, I think after all the city is receiving fair and generous treatment from the government.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Would the minister be
prepared to do for other cities what it is doing for Ottawa?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT
speechtext:
I believe we
would be prepared to do the same for any other city in which the capital might be located.

Now, Mr. Chairman, mark you, the loss to the farmers on fourteen farm products only during the five years this government has been in power is $2,000,000,000. Now the government say to the farmers, We will save you by lending you $90,000,000. A nice proportion. This is how they are going to save the farmers. They are proud of their legislation. Some help! Great help, great assistance for those people who in the words of the Prime Minister have shown so much fortitude during these years of stress. Fortitude! They need help; he gives them words. But unfortunately they cannot swallow them

as well as the Prime Minister swallows his own words. And it is better for them not to swallow the words that come from the government because they would make them sick. Here we have this legislation to lend $90,000,000 to the farmers. They need money, but would it not be better if the finance minister came to the house with other legislation, to remove the tariff barriers that prevent the farmers from trading with the other countries of the world.
Who will pay for this? Will the farmer be self-sustaining with that legislation? No, sir, because the finance minister answering the hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. Gray) said, The farmer will have to pay that money back to the government. And that surely is a business proposition. But will it put the farmer on his feet? No, sir. Just humbug once more, just bluff. It is just an expedient to get past election time and afterwards the farmer will not be any better off than before. The government comes with legislation to serve as steps to enable the farmer to get over the tariff wall, but there are no steps and no ladder for him to come down, therefore the farmer is in danger of breaking his neck coming down the high tariff wall that has been built by this government. Sir, although it is necessary to come to the rescue of the farmer I find this legislation silly. If the government had been wise enough, the tariff barriers would have been destroyed and the farmer would not have had to get over this wall, he would have been able to pass through. The only blasting that the Prime Minister should do is to blast his own tariff walls, this would be the most sensible thing.

This is what. I do not understand. If the members of the government are sincere in saying that they earnestly wish the welfare of the farmer there is only one thing for them to do, that is to repair the wrongs that they themselves have done to the farmer. This is what should be done. They can do that very easily; they have only to cancel the silly legislation which has been forced upon this house by their brute majority. That is the only thing which they have to do, and if it is done this bill will be superfluous. If that is not done, next year whatever government is in office will have to loan the farmers much more money, unless the tariff walls are demolished.
That is the situation. Now I should like to ask a question of the minister who, as I say, is a very sensible man, and who in addition possesses manners, which is something that counts. The farmers of this country have lost two billion dollars on the sale of only fourteen farm products during the five years this government has been in power. I should like to ask the minister how the farmers who have lost so much because of the policies of this government will be made more comfortable by being able to borrow a sum which does not represent even one-half of one per cent of their losses. They have lost two billion dollars; you offer to loan them $90,000,000. That does not amount to even one-half of one per cent on their losses on only fourteen farm products. Far from being exaggerated my figure does not represent the actual loss, since it does not cover everything produced on the farm. The minister knows very well that we do not exaggerate the problems and worries of the farmers, and he knows very well that less than one-half of one per cent of their losses will not give the farmers very great comfort or help. Quite so, but that is not
money at cost; that is money at less than cost. I stated the other day that it should be the policy of the government to loan money to the farmers at a rate as low as possible consistent with the general well being of the country at large and of the farmer himself. I can see another very grave danger. There would be an inducement to many farmers whom I know personally to have not a dollar of mortgage upon their property to seek to get money at 3| per cent when they could turn around and loan it in their own neighbourhood at 5J and 6 per cent. We must look at these things in a practical way, and I believe as much harm as good would be done by loaning money to the farmers at such a low rate. Having said so much let me repeat that I should like to see the farmer get his money at as low a rate as is consistent with the general interest, including his own interest.
On that point let me say that in the United States where, as is well known, they have been very generous with public funds under the land banks which were set up for the purpose of loaning government money to farmers. At the present moment they charge b\ per cent, with the proviso that for a period until 1938, I think, the money is subject to a lowering of the interest rate by one-half per cent. Under the agreements they pay 5 per cent until 1938 and after that they pay 5A per cent. Even where the government loans money to cooperative associations of farmers set up in communities, where these farmers in turn guarantee the mortgage of each individual farmer, that money is loaned to the associations at the rate of 5 per cent, and in addition the farmer must make a subscription of 5 per cent to the stock of the association, which means that his interest is increased to the extent that interest would be added to that 5 per cent.

We have every reason to expect that in Canada we will have money for the farmer at 5 per cent.

Mr. Chairman, I believe the intention behind the legislation passed in 1927 was to loan money to farmers so that they would be in a position to carry on their farming operations. I believe, further, that it was the intention to loan money at as low a rate as possible, having regard to the cost of operation. It seems to me that an entirely different situation prevails to-day from that which obtained in 1927. At that time it appeared good business policy to loan money to farmers for purposes of production and for the general extension of farming operations. So far as my personal knowledge of present conditions in Saskatchewan goes, however, it would seem a first class policy not to loan money under prevailing circumstances to any farmers. I speak for the prairie provinces, with which I am more familiar. I make that statement because today the farmer cannot pay the interest on loans made to him, nor has he been able to do so for the past three or four years. I do favour the legislation however because I believe we are acting wisely when we attempt to make money available for the farmer who finds himself confronted with a considerable overhead of debt at a high rate of interest.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
I should like to urge upon the Minister of Finance the necessity for the government to carry the costs of administration of farm loans. They are carrying the administration costs in connection with the measure for unemployment insurance, they carry the administration costs in connection with old age pensions, and they have to carry the costs in other instances. Under present conditions in agriculture the Farm Loan Act is in the nature of a relief measure set up to relieve the farmer in his difficulties. As the government may know short of a straight bonus difficulty is found in finding ways of helping the farmer directly, and I suggest that we now have before us the means for helping him.
A very great percentage of farmers have some debt. Although not all have mortgages against their property, many would like very much to take out a small mortgage in order to settle irritating debts, grocery bills, doctor bills, twine bills, machinery bills and other bills they may have to meet. There would be no use offering them a loan at five per *cent or five and one-half per cent because they would not be able to pay the debt. The legislature of the province of Ontario proposes to pay one per cent, thereby lowering the rate to four and one-half per cent. Even at that rate however agriculture could not pay. To-day we are facing new conditions, conditions we have never met before, and whether we must spend a great amount of money or not I feel that the federal government could best serve agriculture by carrying the administrative costs of the farm loan operations thereby, according to the statement of the Minister of Finance, cutting the interest rates by one and one-half per cent.
It is true, further, that government policies, such as tariff and immigration policies and exchange rates affect farmers' prices. We know that world conditions affect the prices the farmer receives and in many cases the cost of his requirements. I believe it is admitted that government policy in the past has not been of a kind likely to assist the farmer of to-day. I believe it is admitted that the policy of solicited immigration which has obtained, until recently, for the past thirty years or more has not led to any improvement
Farm Loan Act

in the present condition of the farmer. I believe it is admitted, further, that high tariffs have been detrimental to his interests, and that an exchange rate which did not place Canadian money on a par with British money in the first year or so in which this government held office undoubtedly adversely affected farmers' prices. And so all these things being true I feel, though it may seem a radical departure and to the minister may even seem in many ways an unwise step, that it would be much better, to carry the administration costs and thus enable the farmer to pay interest on his loans than it would be to load him with the administration costs as well as four per cent, making 5i per cent altogether, which he is entirely unable to pay and, as time will prove, will not pay. I am sure that the minister wants the loans repaid and the interest payments kept up, and for that reason I feel that it would be better for the government to assume this responsibility. Indeed why should the government not assume the responsibility for agriculture's load just as much as it assumes responsibility for the administration of these other measures, such as unemployment insurance, which does not affect agriculture at all except adversely, and old age pensions, and so on. If it is true then that other groups of citizens should be served by having the administration costs carried by the federal government I can see no reason at all why the same service should not be given to farmers in this their day of extremity.

Certainly on this bill, as I said in the case of the matter brought up by the hon. member for Temiscouata, I do not propose to be drawn into a discussion of that question, but upon another occasion that is a different thing.
My hon. friend has put forward the suggestion that the government should carry the whole administrative costs of the Farm Loan Act. That is a fair subject for discussion. I have in mind the statement made by one member who is himself a farmer, who said that the farmer is not looking for charity. Well, he is getting charity if he asks that the taxpayers of the country at large shall bear the cost of administering the Farm Loan Act. Having said that, I say very frankly to the committee that I have an open mind on the [DOT]question. It might be sound policy to do it;

I am not so sure about that. But when my hon. friend was referring to interest rates she took the rate of five and a half per cent. That is the rate at the moment, but as I have said, I think we can safely anticipate a rate of five per cent or possibly a little lower. But let us take five per cent. Until the suggestion was made to-day by the hon. member for South Batt.leford the lowest rate I have heard mentioned here is four per cent. Everybody has been pleading for four per cent money. My hon. friend from Southeast Grey quite properly pleads the case of the poor farmer who has not a mortgage on his land but has some debts and wants to compound them and take a small mortgage on his farm. I presume she means a mortgage of $1,000. If she does- I may say that the average of all farm loans in Canada is slightly above $2,000,-the difference between four and five per cent for a $1,000 mortgage would be $10 a year. Well, Mr. Chairman, while I sympathize with the farmer every day as I do with many others in all walks of life because of their sufferings and trials and difficulties due to this period through which we are passing, you cannot tell me that $10 is going to make the difference between the success or failure of a farmer who is a farmer on any farm. I only say that in passing. I do not know that I stress it, but we must look at these things in their proper perspective.
I come back to the question of the cost of administration. It is a fair subject for debate, although I must say this, that I still have the feeling that if we put out mortgage money at 3} per cent we would make a grave mistake from the national point of view and the viewpoint of the farmer himself. I may be all wrong about that, but that is my opinion.

speechtext: It may, so far as the immediate future is concerned, but if that farmer is placed on his feet by reason of the operations of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, and is given new courage and a new outlook, and especially with improved conditions as we have a right to expect, I believe that in the natural course of events he can rehabilitate himself so that his credit will depend upon the manner in which he conducts himself in the future. Another amendment is for this purpose: At the present moment in virtue of the amendments passed last year to the Farm Loan Act we are authorized to make loans up to fifty per cent on the land and twenty per cent on the buildings. We now propose to make it fifty per cent on land and buildings. And to indicate the favourable nature of that amendment, may I point out that under the existing legislation in the United States they lend only fifty per cent on land and twenty per cent on buildings. Another amendment provides that the five per cent which has hitherto been subscribed by the farmer shall be credited immediately to his account. That means in effect that he will be saved interest on that sum from this date on. Then there is another amendment designed to meet a situation which arises in the province of Quebec. It will be recalled that last year, in providing for second mortgages, we authorized the board to take in addition chattel mortgages. But they have no chattel mortgages in Quebec; and whereas we can loan up to sixty-six and one-half per cent where chattel mortgages can be taken under the act, where they cannot be obtained, as in the province of Quebec, it would restrict the opportunity of loaning in that province. And so we propose there, notwithstanding the fact that we cannot secure chattel mortgages, to make loans up to sixty per cent. Those are the important provisions.

I rise to support this motion for one reason only; I believe that any legislation put forward by the government to assist the primary producer should be supported by everyone. But after listening, not only this year but during the last three or four years, to what has been said on this subject, I have come to the conclusion that all the help that has been extended to primary producers has been given almost entirely to
Farm Loan Act

farmers, and I do not know what constitutes a farmer. We have swivel chair farmers, speculating farmers, homesteaders and others. If the government intends to pass legislation to assist home builders, then it should receive everyone's support. I would point out to the government however that when we are discussing the necessity of assisting farmers, who are no doubt the backbone of the country, the time has come to give some consideration to those who are handling the other natural products which we have in this dominion. I refer to fishing, lumbering and mining; no assistance has been given to these industries. Three years ago this parliament assisted the farmers of Canada to the extent of five cents a bushel on the wheat they raised, and those who produced wheat were assisted, but those who produced no wheat got no assistance. Consequently that was a failure. Another scheme was tried of assisting the farmers by giving so much per acre, and I understand that also was a failure. Now the government comes along with $90,000,000 to help agriculture, to provide loans on farms at a cheaper rate of interest. But I think-and there are others who feel the same way-that vhe more money you lend to the farmers the more difficult their situation becomes; some classes of farmers should not get any more money. We have tried assisting the farmers- those from the west will pardon me for saying so-and I think we should now try to help some other industry in Canada as well. I am going to support this legislation, but I do submit to the government that they should give some consideration to the other natural products of which I have spoken.

speechtext:
I will not quarrel with the
minister over that, but I do say that the real reason why so little credit is and has been available for farmers in the last three or four years is the collapse of farm prices. I do not need to give a lot of statistics to show what has happened, but I have here a copy of a statement which was received by one of my neighbours in connection with a cow he sent to Calgary in the summer of 1934. It was sent to Adams, Wood & Weiller, live stock commission agents, on July 18, 1934. The cow weighed 870 pounds and brought a price of 50 cents per hundred. The freight on 870 pounds at 30 cents represented$2.61; yardage,35 cents;

Farm Loan Act
hay, 30 cents; yard fire insurance, 5 cents; commission 75 cents; brand inspection, 10 cents. All these charges came to $4.16, and the total selling price was $4.35, which left the farmer with 19 cents for his cow. On the bottom of the statement there is this note: "Please call at the office the next time you are in town and we will give you this credit in cash. We cannot very well issue a cheque for this amount." When that neighbour was discussing this question at the table one day, one of the men said to him, "It is a good job they did not send you that cheque." He said, "Why"? The man replied, " Well, you would have had to pay fifteen cents exchange on it and probably thirty cents for a telephone call to Calgary to see whether there were sufficient funds for the cheque." The minister said a little while ago that he could not believe one per cent difference on the interest rate was such a vital matter as some hon. members had been trying to make out. There was a time when this cow would have brought this man nineteen dollars. This summer she brought nineteen cents. It is true she was a canner cow.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext: Did he cash the cheque?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
No, because he did not get
it. I said to him, " Why are you so anxious to get this cheque"? He said, "I am anxious to frame it, and if when my young son grows up he complains about the price of farm products I shall show it to him and say: You have no kick coming because this was the price I once got." The commission man got 75 cents while the man on the farm got nineteen cents for the cow.
There have been other instances nearly as bad. I remember two years ago last summer when I went home, a five gallon can of No. 1 churning cream brought ninety cents; that is about eighteen cents a gallon for cream. Someone can work out how much that means for a quart of milk. A returned soldier was trying to make a living milking cows. He said that one day as he was milking he endeavoured to figure out how much he was getting for his work, and he came to the conclusion it meant about five hundred pulls for a cent. Farm prices have dropped so low that in many cases there is no possibility of the farm paying its way and had it not been for the protective legislation put on the statute books by some of our provincial governments, thousands of farmers would before this have been in the cities and the provincial governments and municipalities would have been taking care of them under the unemployment relief act. That is the only result there could have been.
In the United States where they did not have protective legislation there were farmers' strikes in some places and in one case the agent of a loan company who came down to a sale to bid in the farm had a rope put around his neck and was threatened with hanging. That kind of thing might have happened in some provinces had there not been protective legislation. Conditions got so bad that legislation of that kind was unavoidable. The men in charge of some of these big companies that have so many millions of dollars at stake in farm mortgages never showed any intelligent interest in this question; I never heard any of them make any suggestion to the farmer except that he reduce his production costs, tighten his belt and work a little harder. I never heard of them tightening their own belts. As for some of those heads of insurance companies drawing $50,000 a year in salaries, I never heard of them offering to reduce their own salaries. We in parliament could have done something for the farmer and we did not do it. Over four years ago I urged upon the house the necessity for doing something, abandoning the gold standard and stopping this deflation that was going on in Canada. I have been urging this every year since; I know I have made myself a nuisance to some hon. members. A couple of years ago one of them said to me: "Why are you always yapping so much about Australia"? If it is not out of place at this time I would like to take five or ten minutes to tell the house what conditions might have been like if we had gone even as far as Australia has done.
Before I do that may I point out that in 1929 the net revenue -of the farms of Canada was $1,034,000,000, but in 1932 it was only $425,000,000 or 40 per cent, while the volume of production in 1932 was 14 per cent greater than in 1929. From 1929 to 1932 the average farm income was reduced from approximately $1,500 to approximately $600. The farmer, however, was still required to make the same payments on his overhead and his debts in 1932 that he had in 1928, and the money was not there. Therefore I do not wonder that credit facilities dried up. No man will give credit to the farmer if he cannot see any possibility of getting his money back.
Australia adopted an entirely different policy from that adopted in Canada. Not only did they reduce the rate of interest by legislation, which we did not do, but they allowed their currency to depreciate in outside countries. This was part of a national plan, a deliberate depreciation of their currency. They abandoned the gold standard in 1930, five years

speechtext:
I am not able to get any figures for the volume of production in Australia but I will give the volume in Canada just in a moment. The total actual gross value of production in Canada for the three years 1931, 1932 and 1933 was 12,382,000,000, if the percentage drop had been the same as it was in Australia our total gross production would have been $3,424,000,000. The actual figure being $2,382,000,000, it shows a loss in our gross production of $1,042,000,000. I estimate the loss for 1934 at $300,000,000. I have no figures to verify it, because the figures for Australia are not available at the moment, but assuming that sum, for the sake of the argument, it gives a total of $1,342,000,000. That is what I would consider the drop in gross value of agricultural production because of the fact that we have not been on a comparative exchange basis with Australia.
There is a difference in the figures given by our bureau of statistics between gross value and net value in agricultural production, because in the gross value there is much duplication. For instance field products are valued separately from live stock, but a large percentage of field products are fed to live stock. The bureau give net figures as well as gross; and for 1931, 1932 and 1933 their figures of net production are 63 per cent of gross production. Taking therefore 63 per cent of the estimated loss of $1,342,000,000 would give an estimated loss in net revenue to Canadian farmers in these four years, due to the difference in exchange between Canada and Australia, of $845,000,000. Let me say at once that these are not positive figures; they are based on estimates which have been prepared in both countries by the bureau of statistics.
Coming now to the question raised by the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Young) as to the volume of production: no statistics are available as -to volume in either country so far as I could ascertain, but 1 have the figures for agricultural marketings in Canada, also

Farm Loan Act
secured from the bureau of statistics. Taking 1926 as equal to 100, the agricultural marketings in Canada were:
1929	 101
1931		 99
1932		 114-3
1933		 105-1
This would indicate that the average production for 1931, 1932 and 1933 was somewhat greater than in 1929, so we can say that the drop in the value of production in Canada was not due to a decrease in volume. I have only taken into account the difference in the money income to the Canadian farmer because of this exchange situation, but that is the important point when dealing with the question of debts and interest. In Australia in the fall of 1932, due to the difference in exchange and the resulting difference in the price of wheat, and due also to the legislation in Australia reducing interest rates by 22J per cent, of the existing rate 100 bushels of wheat would pay the interest for one year on a mortgage drawn for $1,000 at 8 per cent interest, whereas in Canada it would take 200 bushels to pay the interest on a similar mortgage. That is the reason the Canadian farmers could not pay their interest; it took too much of their product, for of course the only way a farmer can pay any interest is from the product of his farm. If in order to pay his interest he has to drive three times as many steers or hogs to market or deliver twice as many bushels of wheat, he is not going to have as much for himself. Under the conditions of the last few years a farmer could not pay the interest or reduce the principal, and in many cases he could not even pay his taxes.
I want to go a little further. In addition to the increased ability of the Australian farmer to pay debts or fixed charges, he also had a large advantage in purchasing power or real income. The statistics are not quite up to date, but in March, 1932, using the March, 1930, figures in both countries as equalling 100-these figures were worked out for me by the bureau of statistics here-the purchasing power of farm products in Australia gave an index figure of 96-1, whereas in Canada the figure was 68-6. In other words the purchasing power of farm products in Australia was 40 per cent greater than in Canada.
In June, 1934, on the basis of 1913 prices equalling 100 in both countries, the purchasing power of farm products in Australia and Canada was as indicated by the following figures:

These figures indicate that the purchasing power of farm products in Australia was 25 per cent greater than it was in Canada. There you have a pretty good indication of the cause of the present farm debt situation and the reason why reasonable credit facilities are not available to farmers in Canada to-day.
Until the present deflation I do not think there was any field of- investment in Canada that Showed a better record, outside of government bonds, as far as losses to the investor are concerned, than farm mortgages. But during the last five years we have gone through conditions that in many cases made payment absolutely impossible. Even yet I do not think the default in farm mortgages is as great as it has been in connection with corporation bonds. I have a statement here which shows that corporation bond defaults in Canada during the last four years total over $500,000,000, which I believe is twenty-five per cent of all the corporation bonded debt in Canada. Then I have a statement of the default in municipal bonds, which shows a total for 1934 of over $118,000,000, made up as follows:

There is another question that I wish now to bring to the attention of the Minister of Finance and the committee, namely, what has been done in other countries in regard to this matter of credit for farmers. I feel safe in stating that farm mortgages in Canada are carrying at the present time a higher rate of interest than in almost any other country, certainly any of our competitors. A great many people in my constituency are still paying eight per cent, some nine per cent. If the minister has any fuller information in regard to rates in other countries to-day I hope he will give it to the committee. In New Zealand in 1932 they had a National Expenditure Adjustment Act, under which there was a reduction of interest rates on mortgages, as well as of rents and other fixed charges, to five per cent on real estate mortgages and six and one-half per cent on chattel mortgages. The court was also given power to postpone payments and to reduce interest rates and principal and to remit arrears of principal in whole or in part.

We are sticking to the bill, and sticking strictly to' the bill. What I have said has a very direct and definite relationship with the whole argument of the Minister of Finance on this bill. He has suggested that the hon. member for Macleod is to be rebuked because he used illustrations from other countries, notably New Zealand and Australia, to point the moral of his tale. I heard the Prime Minister himself for hours and for days pointing the moral of his tale by holding out the unemployment insurance measure of Great Britain. That is a distant pasture, almost as distant as Australia or New Zealand.
If it comes to a question of distant pastures this government should not rebuke anybody. It was the government's anxiety to guard the well being of New York and other foreign creditors which resulted in the deliberate action of maintaining currency at a fictitious
Farm Loan Act

value in relation to international exchange and which resulted in a ghastly loss to us, as I stated formerly. The hon. member for Macleod has put up an argument which the minister has not and cannot answer. I do hope however that in spite of that the government will consider the advisability of helping to carry the costs of the administration of this bill. I hope before the bill is given third reading the government will have become sufficiently well advised to introduce a clause such as has been introduced in connection with the unemployment insurance measure. Subsection (3) of section 8 of the unemployment insurance measure contains the following provision:
The costs of administration of this act, including remuneration of commissioners, officers, clerks and employees, shall be paid out of moneys provided by parliament.
I submit the inclusion of a section exactly the same as the one I have read would enable the farm loan board to advance moneys to agriculture at a rate of interest which would be in some degree commensurate with the farmers' ability to pay.

speechtext:
I am pleased the minister has made the correction. One of the contributing factors of limitation of the farmers' borrowing powers has 'been the debt adjustment acts of the different provinces.

Farm Loan Act
The de'bt adjustment act of the province of Manitoba, with which I am most familiar, does nob go as far as the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. All the debt adjustment act of that province means is a postponement of the conditions; they have no power to write down. It is simply a postponement, and eveiry person who comes under the act in the province of Manitoba must put his cards on the table aDd give a true statement of his affairs. If he does not do so the debt adjustment board will not protect him. We know however that the farmers in western Canada who are not and never have been operating under a debt adjustment act at certain periods of the year want to borrow small sums of money to buy twine or other articles connected with production, and they find it impossible to borrow the small sums necessary. They cannot borrow it from the banks-and may I say I do not blame the banks. The condition is that a farmer with one hundred or two hundred acres of grain ready for the binder cannot get S30 or $40 to buy twine. But when the resolution was before the house I took the stand that the amendment to the Farm Loan Act should be complementary to the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. I stated the impression had been created in western Canada that the Farm Loan Act of 1934 was complementary to the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, and many farmers were under the impression that if they went before a receiver and had their debts adjusted they could, go to the farm loan board and borrow the amount due after the readjustment had been made. They were further of the opinion that if they had to go before a board of review, such board having power to make a compromise despite the views of the creditors or debtors, they could use the farm loan board for purposes of consolidating their debts. The minister rather doubted that that opinion could exist. The minister distinctly said that the Farm Loan Act was going to be run along business lines and he could see no reason why the farmers in any part of the country should get the opinion that these amendments to the Farm Loan Act would be complementary to the debt adjustment act. But I have the Prime Minister with me. It is not very often, but I have him with me this time, for here is what he said in 1934 when he proposed the resolution that it is expedient to amend the Canadian Farm Loan Act:
I endeavoured to indicate to the house this afternoon in a broad and general way that this bill is complementary to the bill dealing with the adjustment of farm indebtedness.
Then further on he makes this statement:
I also indicated that the measure founded upon the resolution contemplates that additional advances to those already provided for in the provisions of the Canadian Farm Loan Act may be made, to enable a scheme of composition or arrangement to be carried into effect.
I know the Minister of Finance is a fair-minded man, except when some hon. member gets under his skin, and I do not think he could get any other impression from the words of the Prime Minister than what the farmers in western Canada got, namely, that immediately the machinery created by this parliament to make a debt compromise was available, together with this other machinery, providing 870,000,000 or $90,000,000, the farmer could go and use this other piece of machinery and consolidate his debts. I am still of opinion-I have not changed my mind at all-that if the Farm Loan Act and the debt adjustment act are going to work the benefits for the farmer that the minister and the government expect, they must work in conjunction. If they do not I doubt very much the success of these two pieces of legislation.
May I say this to the minister before taking my seat? The echoes of the Farm Loan Act and the debt adjustment act were heard throughout the country last year. In fact, politicians were going around saying that the farmers could borrow from the farm loan board at no more than five per cent interest. Now in 1935, with an election on the horizon, the minister can readily imagine what the supporters of the present government will be spreading around in the country to the farmers. They will point out that the legislation that was brought down last year was amended this year, increasing the amount available, and the minister who is a fair-minded man generally, can imagine what will be broadcast to the farmer, giving the impression much more strongly even than last year that both acts are designed to work together.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I do not think it is necessary for the hon. member for Provencher to quote the Prime Minister in support of his assertion that the amendment to the Farm Loan Act wa3 intended to be complementary to the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act.

speechtext: I thought he was a good authority.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
My hon. friend apparently had the idea in his mind that he was controverting some position that I had taken. I have never for one moment suggested that the
Farm Loan Act

Farm Loan Act was not to be regarded as complementary to the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. Quite the contrary. What I did say was this. I am not sure whether the suggestion came from the hon. member for Macleod or some other hon. member, but it was suggested that we should make an amendment whereby it would be obligatory on the farm loan board ipso facto to loan money provided that the board of review under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act said they were to do so, I pointed out how illogical that would be, that you could not have one body issuing orders upon another responsible body. I said that each individual case would have to be dealt with by the farm loan board on its merits, and the farmer who has an adjustment made under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act can still get his loan from the farm loan board, but not as a matter of right. The discretion must rest with the farm loan board, as to the man, the character of his farm, the probabilities of his succeeding and other necessary factors. But if he is a good farmer, a worthy farmer, with reasonable security, he will have no difficulty in securing money under those circumstances from the farm loan board. But I wanted to dispel the idea that simply because a farmer comes and knocks at the door he must of necessity gain admittance. That would do away with all discretion on the part of the board, and we could not hold them responsible for the handling of public funds.

speechtext: I am very glad to have this statement from the minister because now I shall be in a position in the next campaign, if any of his supporters try to create the impression that they did last year, to quote the minister's own words in denial.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
I usually find, even though I do not agree with all his premises, that I do agree with the logic of the Minister of Finance, but I am compelled to say that I could not quite follow the logic of his position when he replied to the hon. member for Macleod that any discussion of the monetary policies of this and other countries in their relation to farm prices had not a very close relation to the bill now under discussion.
After all, what was the suggestion of the hon. member for Macleod? The suggestion was that the government of the day might well insert a provision in this act that the administrative costs of the farm loan board and of the Farm Loan Act should be borne from public funds. In pointing out that this was a responsibility which the government might well assume, . the hon. member for

Macleod also pointed out that to a degree at least other policies of the government were responsible for the necessity of the provisions of this bill. He pointed out, as I understood him, that one of those policies which had made this bill essential, which had decreased the value of farm credit and had made it difficult for the farmer to borrow money through the ordinary channels, and made it difficult for the farmer to pay anything but the lowest interest rate, was the policy of deflation which had been followed by this country, followed in the opinion of the government in the direct interests of the nation itself. Certainly with my limited powers of logic, Mr. Chairman, I thought the argument was one which had an absolute relation to the matter in hand and one which might well have been answered, although I will admit at once that I would not expect the minister to go into any detailed discussion at this time of the policies of inflation or deflation.
But there is another point which has to be considered, and after all it is the foundation fact. What is the purpose of the legislation? As I see it, it is twofold: First, to provide for farmers a credit which they otherwise might not receive, to make available to them a source of credit which is made necessary by reason of the fact that private commercial credit is no longer available to them. Secondly, to establish some form of interest control, indirectly, by loaning that money at as low a rate as possible. Now the question arises at once, what is a reasonable rate? That, as has been stated again and again, and as I think the minister will accept, must depend on two factors; one is the cost of the money, and the other is the ability to pay. Many arguments have been advanced to show that the farmer's ability to pay has been greatly reduced. As a matter of fact I can go a little further. The reduction in price levels and farm values is accompanied by much more than a corresponding reduction in ability to meet interest charges, because after all while interest charges are paid out of prices they are paid only out of that proportion of the price received for production which is over and above the cost of operation and of living. The lower the price the less the proportion of production which is left available for meeting the payment of debts or taxation, and the greater the proportion of that production that must be absorbed in ordinary operation and living cost, so that the proportion available for debt is smaller, and the value of each item of that proportion is smaller. The debt paying ability of the farmer is therefore reduced

Farm Loan Act
by far more than the percentage of price reduction. I believe I am following closely logical reasoning in this.
Now we come to the point of the government's responsibility in the matter. I will not say, because I think it is unfair to say, that the government has a definite responsibility to perform any service for any part of the community at the cost of the state itself. But the government has set in many instances the precedent of having accepted that responsibility, and the precedent which has been cited again and again, the precedent most recently discussed in this house, that of unemployment insurance, is very much in point. That is a policy which in the national interest must be put into effect, but it is a policy which will directly benefit only a limited percentage of the population of the country. And yet it is a policy towards the support of which every part of the country must contribute, so far as state expenditure is concerned. I have no quarrel with that, because I believe that in a large way if anything is really good for any part of the community it must be good for the community as a whole.

speechtext: Oh, no.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
And I think the
reverse is also true. But if in the long run it is really good, if it is sound, and raises one part of the community to a proper level, it will have a corresponding beneficial effect on all other parts of the country. Now if that is so, when we turn to agriculture I can see no logical reason why the same process should not be followed. It is just as much in the national interest that agriculture should be on a reasonable basis, that it should be able to meet its obligations and continue to operate, as it is that there should be unemployment insurance for those who in the future may be unfortunate enough to lose their job. To my mind it is even more important, because the maintenance of agriculture on a proper basis means the maintenance of increased wealth in the nation as a whole. The maintenance of the unemployed on a basis of reasonable insurance is much more individual in effect, except in so far as it will reduce the cost of unemployment relief and maintain the morale, the decent citizenship and! the moral; standards of those affected.
It is unnecessary for me to stress the fact that the lowest possible rate of interest is all, and sometimes indeed more than all that the farmers can pay. Of such paramount importance is this question of interest that it is worth the government's while to look
upon it as a definite national policy to be supported to a degree, at least so far as administrative cost is concerned, by national expenditure, towards which the farmers themselves will contribute their mortgage, which is more than can be said for the unemployment insurance measure; because the larger part of the state's contribution under that measure will be paid by those who receive no benefit from the fund.
It is all very well for the minister to say that, taking a mortgage of $1,000, one per cent means only $10, which is not much. Well, in some instances $10 means a good deal, but apart from that it is not just $10. The average mortgage debt, at least in the west where farms are larger, is much more than $1,000; and if you multiply that $10 by two, three, four or five, as it is multiplied right through, then that $30, $40 or $50 may mean the difference between the ability of the farmer to meet his obligation and his inability. And if he can meet it it may spell the difference between a reasonable standard of comfort and a standard far below par. The next important point is this-and I am glad to see that the minister has it in contemplation, although of course no act is any stronger than its subsequent administration, and no minister can say definitely how an act will be administered; he can only indicate the lines along which it should be administered and, to the best of his ability, safeguard its administration through legislation. You can have a poor act and it may run fairly well if it is in the hands of first class men with first class policies; and on the other hand the best act may be unsatisfactory if it is administered by the wrong men with wrong ideas. To my mind it is imperative to meet one of the greatest abuses, one of the greatest weaknesses of the old act; and after all we are discussing the weaknesses of the old act. And this was one of the greatest of its weaknesses: that the factor the minister has laid down again and again as one of the important features in the lending of money, the moral factor, the question of the type of man himself, had never to my knowledge [DOT] been taken into consideration under the old administration At least I can say this, that time and again, in scores of instances, hopeful borrowers have come to ask my advice as to the best way of presenting their case, and I have had a good many cases laid before me of intending borrowers who were refused a loan. And so far as I could discover, judging from the correspondence, the letters sent by the provincial boards-because, as the minister understands, there is no direct application to
Farm Loan Act

the federal board, and I am not discussing the board under the old act, for it was the provincial board that took that responsibility -never in a single instance have I read or heard of the slightest reference having been made to the personal character, the personal ability and the moral standard of the man himself. It was always a question of tangible security. I am glad therefore that the minister stressed the character of the borrower. That is the greatest criterion. The second is this, and it is a weakness which I hope the government will rectify. I refer to the habit that has persisted through the years of blanketing various areas within which no loan would be made on any terms. I represent one of the better areas in the west, an area which generally speaking has a reasonable rainfall and in which the type of farming carried on is as a rule looked upon as the best foundation for loans-the moderate sized farm in which there is mixed farming, plenty of stock, cattle, hogs, and all the various forms of agriculture, with a good record of production. And yet in that area, in district after district, no loans could be made, no matter what the value of the farm or the character of the man might be. The answer has always been: (Generally speaking, your area is not one of which we approve. The man may be all right, but it is not worth while; it will cost too much to take his application and examine it on its own merits.
I believe the whole scheme should prove a success if the administration is carried on as is contemplated in the act and as is indicated by the minister's statement, that is that there shall be no blanketing of cases, but that each ease shall be taken on its individual merits, as it should be; that the moral character, the spirit, the personality of the man himself will be one of the controlling factors and above all that a generous spirit shall be shown in the administration of the act. If you have that, coupled with what I believe is absolutely sound, the lowest possible rate of interest made available-and I think that is a sound stand to take

by the assumption on the part of the state of the administrative costs of this act just as the administrative costs of other acts have been taken over by the state, so that the farmers who do borrow will have the same rate as that at which the state can borrow, the effect of that low rate of interest will be so reflected in commercial rates as to carry the benefit far beyond the bounds of the act itself. After all-and this to my mind should never be lost sight of-I have heard lenders, mortgage companies and others state again and again

that the high rates of interest on farm mortgages in western Canada were rendered necessary because of the insecurity of the loan; that is, they had to have a higher rate in order to. cover possible losses. Yet it has been driven home again and again that the greatest single factor in making a loan insecure is a rate of interest beyond that which the money will earn in that particular business; that is what makes a loan insecure. I am taking it for granted that the loan in the first place is made to the proper type of person engaged in the proper type of industry and with reasonable security. I am not afraid the farm loan board or any other will go outside those factors in making loans, but taking for granted those factors, the biggest one that tends to insecurity of loan, of repayment, is charging a rate of interest beyond that which the man can earn in the business during the term of years the money is loaned. The government would be well advised, realizing this fact, to take over, for the time being at least and until prices reach a reasonable level, the cost of administration.

means of obtaining a loan from the federal farm loan board, there was nothing to compel him to do so.

The property for which exemptions from seizure are now provided, and for which farmers would be asked to waive exemption rights as a means of getting a loan would include:

The question I would like to ask the minister is this:	Have the exemption laws in
any or all of the provinces where they have such laws been waived in order to make the act operative in such provinces? Because if they have been, it seems to me that it is rather, shall I say, a drastic step to take. In Saskatchewan the movement from the dried out areas to the northern portion of the province would not have been possible had it not been for the exemption laws in operation in that province; that is to say, farmers who were down and out claimed under the exemption law enough chattels to permit them to move into some other portion of the province or of the country and start anew. In view of the rather broad exemptions from seizure provided under the terms of your provincial laws it is apparent that the additional security afforded by a mortgage on live stock and' equipment in your province would be of little additional value as security to the board. For the above reasons I am of opinion that the suggested changes in legislation are advisable in order that the security taken on personal property would be of the same relative value to the board in your province as in other provinces.
