Surely that is a mere bagatelle for the government to pay in view of the fact that under the legislation we were considering during most of last week the farmers will bear a very substantial share of the cost of administration which, according to the' Prime Minister at page 941 of Hansard, will amount to approximately $7,000,000 annually. I utterly fail to see why it is not possible for the government to go even much further than the cost of administration in this case. I submit the farmer should not have to pay over four per cent. I am not objecting to the other proposition at all, that the country should bear the administration cost of the unemployment insurance measure, which is expected to amount to about $7,000,000, but I do say that surely it is a very moderate and most reasonable request from those representing the people in the rural districts to ask the government to bear the cost of this measure as well. I may say to my hon. friend that the farmers are suffering much more than the people who have employment, who are the people that will be affected by the unemployment insurance measure. Of course the man on the farm always has employment; the difference between him and some of the other employees is that frequently he gets very little if anything for his work. That is the condition at the present time. I hardly think my hon. friend meant to suggest that in making our request we were asking charity for the farmer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext: If I might make a correction, with my hon. friend's permission, I did not make any such statement. I merely cited the statement made by an hon. member of the house who is himself a farmer.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext: That the farmers did not want charity?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
I was not uttering it as
my own statement.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
Really I cannot see that
it makes very much difference whether or not my hon. friend was quoting someone else as
(Mr. Rhodes.]
to the farmer not wanting charity; evidently my hon. friend gave the quotation with approval.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext: No.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
I say this is not charity.
It is bare justice. Before we reach the amendments to which my hon. friend has referred I should like him to take this question into consideration. If money can be borrowed at three and a half per cent on long term loans, as my hon. friend suggests, and the cost of administering the $10,000,000 already on loan is only $124,000, that means practically one and a quarter per cent. One and a half per cent would amount to $150,000. Surely that is a very small amount to ask the government to bear in connection with this great industry. I wonder if what has been said regarding the tremendous difficulties under which the agriculturist is labouring is fully appreciated 'by hon. members representing constituencies in which the people are engaged in other industries. The figures I placed upon Hansard a few days ago serve to show that in 1933 the price of farm products was just a little more than fifty per cent of the price in [DOT] 1930. That fact, coupled with the extra overhead, makes the difficulties of the farmer just that much greater. I believe it is time the government came to the rescue in some substantial way. I appreciate what the minister has said about what he is doing to lighten the burdens of the farmers, and I thank him for placing before the committee a memorandum of the amendments he proposes to mpve, one of which will change the definition of the word "farmer," while another would fix all accrued interest at the same rate. I realize those changes would be beneficial. I must- say however that as the province of Ontario has not had any loans under the act a reduction in accrued interest will be of no advantage. The other changes mentioned by the minister really amount to very little if anything so far as helping the farmers is concerned. If there is to a real attempt to stem the tide of migration from the farm to the city, an action which is sorely needed, we must have more than the assistance offered by the amendments the minister has mentioned.
I again urge that the farmer who is borrowing money cannot afford to pay more than four per cent interest. It is no greater charity to reduce the rate the farmer has to pay from five per cent to four per cent than it was to reduce the interest rate the banks had to pay on savings accounts from three to two per cent. I am not objecting to the change, but simply make that observation in passing. I

Farm Loan Act
believe the minister received sympathetically the suggestion for a change in the act whereby the farmer may at any time pay off any amount he may choose. Under the act as it now stands the board may make long term loans to farmers. If there were a clause making the provision I have suggested I believe the arrangement for long term loans could be overcome. At times money may come in from unexpected sources which may be worth to the farmer as much as he is paying to the farm loan board. I do believe some provision along that line should appear in all the mortgages, and would suggest an amendment along those lines.
I do not believe the minister has proposed any change in the scale of fees. I know that the truck or market gardener on the outskirts of a city working probably twenty-five acres of land is suffering a hardship if he has to pay the same fees on a small loan that the farmer on a much greater acreage has to pay for a larger loan. I do not wish to repeat any of the arguments I stressed a feiw days ago, but I believe the great question is that of deciding how much interest the farmer is going to have to pay. I hope that something may have enabled the minister to take a somewhat different view before he puts into effect the amendments he has suggested.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I shall deal first with the last point, lest I forget it. The act already provides that the farmer may pay at any time he wishes, and the regulations of the board amplify the point. It is a practice the (board has always followed.
When referring to the amendments I believe I did not mention the provision for shorter term mortgages. If hon. members will recall they will realize that the whole set-up of the original act provided for long term loans. In the amendment we are providing a discretionary power enabling the board to take shorter term loans. When I use the expression "shorter term" I mean a five year or six year mortgage, rather than a twenty-two year or thirty-five year mortgage for which provision is made in the present act.
The hon. member has laid stress upon the point that the state should bear the cost of administration. Earlier in the proceedings I admitted that the point was debatable, and I believe my stand will indicate my view, namely that it is a fair subject for discussion. I do not believe I need enlarge upon the point, but I must say the hon. member should not refer to 8124,000 as a mere bagatelle; neither should he have that sum in mind when he considers mortgages running up to $90,000,000,
because inevitably while the cost of administration may not rise in exact ratio to the volume of loans, nevertheless it will tend to rise, and for that reason the figure the committee must have in mind is something larger.
The hon. member seems to hold the view that the farmer is called upon to bear a proportion of the general taxation in com neetion with other measures. That may be true, but I would suggest that the hon. member must bear in mind, if he wishes to be logical, that there are tens of thousands of farmers who do not have mortgages on their property, and if we wish to pursue the argument what we are saying is that the farmer who' pays his way and has no mortgage must be subjected to additional taxation in respect of the farmer who has a mortgage. For that reason I do not think it behooves us to pursue that line of argument too far. One hon. gentleman suggested that inasmuch as the state bears the cost of administration under the Old Age Pension Act the farmer should receive a similar benefit under the present measure. I would draw to the attention of the committee however the fact that the farmer participates in the Old Age Pensions Act precisely as does any other man. For that reason it seems to me the argument is not consistent.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext: What about unemployment insurance?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext: There may be a point there; I am not resisting the argument. It may be sound public policy, bearing always in mind the question how far we should go in the matter of interest rates. According to the press reports-I have nothing official with respect to it-the Ontario government has announced that the farmer in Ontario will pay only four per cent on mortgages. If so, my hon. friends need not worry about the farmers of Ontario because they are going to get four per cent money anyway.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext: Four per cent on gilt edged loans; that is up to fifty per cent of the value of the land, and I think twenty per cent of the extra value as a result of buildings. But those are the only loans to which it applies, as I understand it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext: If that is so the offer is not worth a great deal, because gilt edged loans can take care of themselves.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
How could gilt edged loans take care of themselves during the last two or three years?
Farm Loan Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
The answer is obvious. If any loan will take oare of itself, it is the gilt edged loan, even in these days of stress. Notwithstanding the statement which has been made so sweepingly here that the farmer is not in a position to pay his mortgage, let me say that even with the rates of interest as they were, at six and a half per cent under the Farm Loan Act, plus contributions towards the principal by way of amortization, the farmers have paid their interest with remarkable regularity. We have provinces where even under existing conditions the farmers have made their payments promptly to the extent of at least seventy-five per cent. Even in western Canada, where conditions are even more acute owing to circumstances which I need not discuss here, the payments have been made to a remarkable extent. But in stating that-
Mr. MePHBE: Mr. Chairman-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext: I may say to my hon. friend from Yorkton that I happen to have the facts before me.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext: That is not what I had in mind. I was going to say, do not make the same mistake your leader made two or three years ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
I am obliged to my hon. friend for warning me. I have made plenty of mistakes in the past and I have no doubt that I shall make more in the future, but if I am making a mistake in stating what I believe to be a fact, I can assure my hon. friend that I shall make many of them. I was simply proceeding to disclose the facts from the record. If my hon. friend had allowed me to finish my sentence I was going on to say that I did not regard that as indicating that the farmer is not having a difficult time. Far from it. I know that in many instances he is carrying a burden that is too heavy, and I am just as keen as my hon. friend from Yorkton and my hon. friend from West Middlesex to see the burden of taxation lightened. But we must keep a sense of proportion. It is true that we are passing through difficult times, but we must not predicate our legislation upon the assumption that present conditions will always exist. I think we might make the mistake of attempting to do too much for the farmer, with the inevitable result that I endeavoured to indicate in my remarks at an earlier stage.
Having said so much, let me say to my hon. friend again that I am prepared to hear further discussion as to whether it is the part of wisdom to determine as a matter of policy

that the whole cost of administration shall be borne by the state. It must be borne in mind that we should not only be involved in the cost of administration, but inevitably there are bound to be losses, and if there is not some reserve within the administration of the act itself, those losses in addition must be borne by the state.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
In answer to one statement of the minister, in referring to the $90,000,000, may I point out that this act has been in operation for eight years, and as I understand the statement, the total amount loaned in that period is under $10,000,000; in the last year, 1033-34, they have loaned very little aver half a million dollars, and the year before that the amount loaned was $1,276,000. So that unless there is some change in the lending under this act it will ibe a long time before there would be needed any sum that would approximate $90,000,000.
Then as to what the minister said with regard to gilt edged loans taking care of themselves, the regrettable feature about farming conditions at the present time is that gilt edged loans will not take care of themselves. I do not care how good a loan may be, you could go round the best sections of Ontario in the last few years seeking a farm loan and practically everybody would simply say: We are not taking farm loans. It did not make any difference whether it was for fifty or twenty per -cent of the value of the farm. Perhaps I should not say that it did not make any difference, but the answer invariably would be simply:
We are not lending on farms at the present time. I quite agree with the minister that there are great differences in the kinds of security you may get, both real estate and the personal security of the mortgagor. I agree that there are some to whom it is not safe to lend any money, and that there are others to whom you could with safety lend perhaps a little more than fifty per cent on account of their particular ability to pay interest and part of the principal. But when my hon. friend refers to gilt edged farm loans taking care of themselves, that is not the condition that obtains at the present time, except with the farm loan board of Ontario, so far as I know. I am glad to hear the minister say that he is at least considering having the government bear the cost of administration, and I hope the government will go at least that far. .

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
During the life of the old bill we had somewhat of a dual responsibility, and without a great deal of satisfaction. We

Farm Loan Act
were governed here by a board of three trustees, and the finance minister was either chairman or ex officio a member of the board. Then in the provinces there was a farm board manager, plus three trustees, or whatever you like to call them. But under the new act we have a Canadian farm loan board made up of from three to five members, the finance minister not being one of them. We also have a chief executive officer for each province, or more than one, and he has three advisers. I would ask the minister to tell us whether the chief executive officer is to have anything to say at all in regard to the loans, or is he to be simply in the position of advising headquarters at Ottawa? Is Ottawa to have the final say or the Whole say? The old act was very unsatisfactory because if the provincial board did not want to grant a loan they passed the buck to the Ottawa office, and then the Ottawa office passed it back to the province. The offices would seem to be about the same in both bills. I should like to know what the main difference is in the present bill and whether, in view of the fact that the Minister of Finance will not be connected with the board, he will be responsible as he is now to the House of Commons, to answer for the administration of the act.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
The Minister of Finance will be responsible and the government will be responsible to the same extent as they are responsible in connection with the administration of any board which functions under a minister. I did not emphasize the desirability of having the minister of finance removed from the board, but I thought I made it clear that it is quite impossible, in practice and experience, for the minister of finance to find time to attend the numerous sittings of the board and to deal with the various details that will come before it. He has about all he can do to deal with matters of administration without enlarging his activities and getting into actual details of admin-istraton. It is not our desire in this bill to pass the buck, to use the common parlance which we all understand, whether or not we indulge in the game that gave rise to the expression. We want to get away from any such suggestion, and under the new set-up the provincial representative will be an officer of +he board. The policy and final voice will rest with the central board at Ottawa, but in practice it will be tound that the type of man chosen as provincial representative will be a person fully cognizant of the situation in each province and therefore in a position to advise the board with respect to the character of the intended borrower or the
actual borrower as the case might be, and as to the nature of the security. It follows that if a man of the right type, one who carries the confidence of the board, is appointed, his judgment will go a very long way in determining whether an individual borrower shall or shall not secure a loan or, if he does secure it, as to the amount that will be secured. But I do not think it can be contended by any stretch of the imagination that under the circumstances the responsibility will not be that of the board; there can be no question of evading responsibility. The advisory board which it is intended to set up in the provinces is more an honorary board; it is not intended to be at all a salaried body, but a body of men who will carry, I think, the judgment of the people, outstanding men who have the opportunity and willingness to give something of their time to the public service. They are intended to be more largely a consultative body, to guide the provincial representative in dealing with matters affecting lending operations in the individual province.
Mr. McINTOSH; The chairman will be a paid official.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS

If I did not make that point clear the fault is mine. The old provincial board was a body which was selected and appointed by the dominion government by order in council, but it was selected from the nominees of the province in question. In fact, one province, the name of which it is not necessary to mention, insisted that there should be no question of selection but that its nominees should be appointed, and they were; and as a result there has not been the same cooperation between the provincial boards and the federal board that ought to have obtained, giving rise to the suggestion of passing the buck, as my hon. friend from Battle River has said. The advisory body may or may not be called in, but their services will be available should it
Farm Loan Act

be thought desirable to seek this advice for the purpose of assisting the provincial representative.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext: I want to correct the minister on the answer he gave with regard to subsection (h) of section 7, which provides that any borrower may at any time repay the whole or any part of the amount. My thought was that the money might come in shortly after an interest period; it might come from some source not anticipated, and the borrower should have the right, instead of waiting until the end of the year and leaving that money in the savings bank at two per cent while interest was accumulating against him at the rate of five per cent, to repay when he received the money. He cannot do it under this subsection; he can only repay at the interest date. My suggestion was that the money was worth one hundred cents in the dollar at any time to the government, and under these circumstances no loss could possibly occur by receiving it, without waiting for the expiration of the remaining period of the year. There is another question I want to ask the minister and it applies particularly to Ontario. The province, as the agent of this government, ceases to function under this act; that is to say, loans are not being handled by the province.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS

into effect in Ontario the government would be operating through a board set up by the province. Is not that the practice in the various other provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
Under the old act the
provincial board was appointed by the dominion government from a list of nominees submitted by the province, but the whole spirit of the new measure is different. We appoint a provincial representative who will not have any contact with the provincial government.

in operation, then the provincial board disappears. Now this government makes the loan. What about the responsibility for the collection of loans that have been put out by the province up to the coming into effect of this measure?

But when he says that in compensation for that discrimination bare justice can be done the farmer by lowering the interest on those loans to the extent of one per cent by the government paying the cost of administration, I must disagree with him.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext: Then I must be right.

speechtext:
The reduction of one per
cent will not be accepted by the farmers, so far as I can speak for them, as compensation for the discrimination that has prevailed against them in the legislation passed in this house.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext: Partial compensation.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS

Not even partial compensation. It should be remembered that a very small percentage of the farmers of Canada will be able to borrow money under this act, and if that small percentage are given their loans at a lower cost, that in itself will constitute an unfair discrimination against the great bulk of the farmers who will not be able to secure loans under this act.
Before I take my seat there is one question I would1 like to ask the minister. I thought I had made the matter abundantly clear. Farm Loan Act
understood the hon. member for South Battleford clearly and had given me wrong information. subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
If I may judge
by the correspondence I am receiving with regard to this act, the farmers of my district are exhibiting a certain amount of anxiety as to its ultimate application. If my information is correct, when the farm loan act was passed in 1927 the government of Quebec passed enabling legislation and under it a provincial board was formed. When the act was amended last year or two years ago, it was impossible for the province of Quebec to pass enabling legislation in view of the fact that in my province there is no such thing as mortgages on personal or chattel property. I understood the minister this afternoon to say that he was going to correct that situation and raise the amount of the loan from fifty to sixty per cent. I also understand that the five per cent capital subscribed by the province is to be returned. What the people who are writing me are anxious to know is this: if the provincial board is to be abolished, is the machinery provided under provincial agreement to disappear? Is the law as it exists at the present time in Quebec to become void? The minister is, I suppose, aware of the fact that over and above the one and one-half per cent that Quebec subscribes toward interest rate, the provincial government pays the entire cost of the legal work, that is the searching of titles as well as their establishment.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext: No.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
It is all very well
to say no, but I looked up the act a little while ago, and I am right. Anyhow I am asking the minister if what I have stated is the fact, and if so will the coming into force of this act destroy the machinery that at present exists in Quebec for the purpose of helping the farmers not only to search their titles, but to establish their titles and their claims toward securing a loan of some kind? What other machinery will be substituted and to what extent will it replace the machinery that at present exists in Quebec?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
The provincial board will
disappear. The question as to what portion, if any, of the personnel is to be continued is
one rather for the farm loan board. They may or may not be; it depends entirely on the circumstances. So far as I am concerned there will be no decision on that question. The act will be available to the people of Quebec in its new form as fully as, we think more fully than it was in the old, because we are bringing in certain amendments which will widen its opportunity for use in that province. One of the cases in point was referred to by an hon. member. In communications I have had with the Premier of Quebec he has expressed every willingness to cooperate with us in our endeavour to make the act more widely operative in that province, and has met us very fairly in the matter of arranging machinery not so much under this act as under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, and I am very glad to certify to that in this public way.
My hon. friend is in error in saying that the province bears the cost of expenses. It does not. What it has done is to make for a lower scale of fees than obtains in ordinary circumstances, but the cost in Quebec as in all other provinces has been borne by the borrower himself.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
Is it a fact that
an officer was appointed, I think the hon member for Bellechasse, to study the titles, to help the farmers to prepare their cases and so forth? maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
['Mr
Speaker, I appreciate the difficulty that faced the acting Prime Minister (Sir George Perley) when he attempted to reply to the very brilliant speech of my colleague from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie). In view of the fact that his leader, the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) has not announced any definite policy with respect to this important matter of unemployment, and that we have not been able to receive one from the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon), it is not difficult to understand why the acting Prime Minister should simply fall back on what has been the policy of the present government since its inception and say, as the right hon. gentleman did in his closing remarks, that "the question is being considered." I say to you, sir, that it has been considered. I have no doubt that from the very first day this government took office until this hour in the fifth year of their life, and the last I hope, they have been and are still considering this problem. We have no quarrel with the acting Prime Minister when he states that his leader has courage; we agree that he has. But one is reminded of the story of the engineer who, seeing a buffalo bull charging his engine, said " I admire your courage but I cannot admire your judgment." The right hon. gentleman points out to-night the situation that various other countries are facing and points to the fact that Canada has led in this respect. But I would remind him and other hon. members of this house of the fact that in 1930 in reply to members on this side the Prime Minister said that the concern of his party and of the people of Canada was Canada and not the United States or any other country.
I offer no apologies for taking part in this debate. Here we are in 1935 waiting for some definite pronouncement on the part of the government as to how they propose to solve this problem. In 1931 and again in 1932 we were told, as we were told the other night by the Minister of Labour, that the government was waiting to see what the provinces would propose. That might have been all right in 1931 or even in the second session of 1932; but after five years, for the Minister of Labour to come into this house and say that he is waiting to see what the provinces will propose indicates a lack of judgment and of any particular program on the part of the government to solve the problem. In my opinion the time is opportune, indeed it is long overdue, to discuss this problem because during the years this government has been in office it has deliberately delayed the discussion of unemployment relief until the dying days of the
session. This is true of every session. In 1930 they held over our heads the fact that the Prime Minister would not go to the imperial conference unless we rushed the legislation. In 1931 the house began its sittings on March 12 and it was not until July 29, or four days before prorogation, that legislation was introduced in connection with unemployment. In 1931 the act was to expire on March 1, but on March 8 it was extended for two months. In 1933 the Unemployment and Farm Relief Act was introduced on March 21, leaving seven days in which to discuss it. In 1934 the act expired on March 31 and the new act was introduced on March 22, and the house adjourned on March 28 until after Easter, leaving only about four days to discuss the measure, including the time necessary for the Senate to pass it.
I submit therefore that we have a right to bring this matter as forcibly as possibly to the attention of the government in the hope that they will appreciate the problem and take some definite action. I do not wish to weary the house by a repetition of what was promised in connection with unemployment, but it is necessary for one to go back to the election of 1930 in order to bring before the house and the country the steps or lack of steps taken by the government to solve the problem.
On July 10, 1930, speaking at Moncton, the present Prime Minister said:
The Conservative party is going to find work for all who are willing to work, or perish in the attempt. It is going to call parliament at the earliest possible date after July 28 and take such steps as will end this tragic condition of unemployment and bring prosperity to the country ag a whole. . . . Mr. King promises consideration of the problem of unemployment. I promise to end unemployment. Which plan do you like best?
At Victoria on June 17 he said:
We cannot tolerate the dole. Men and women of this country want work, not charity. ... Is there any excuse for Canada to have hard times if the government is discharging its duties as it should?
Then he spoke in Quebec as follows:
There was no necessity for a conference on unemploylment, he continued. The solution was too apparent. "What you want is work," he exclaimed, "not conferences, and you are going to get work." Unless his promises to the People of Canada were kept if elected to office, Mr. Bennett said he wanted Quebec and other members of his party to vote him out of office.
Let me give a brief review of the legislation that has been passed. In 1930, at the special session, some tariff changes were introduced, and the Prime Minister and other speakers on the other side declared that these changes would result in increased employment in', u"Unemployment Relief-Mr. Gray
Canada. Well, looking back over the years that have passed since that time, one cannot help thinking that the \xa720,000,000 then voted for relief at that particular session was but a smoke screen for the raising of the tariff to the height at which it was increased at that special session. Speaking at that time the Prime Minister told us that the numbers of unemployed in Canada were 117,000 as at that date and that it was possible that they might increase during the winter to 177,000. But he told us with all the force at his command that these tariff changes would bring about the employment of at least 25,000 men and thus reduce the number of unemployed. The ex-Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) at that time an earnest admirer of his leader, in whom he said, in 1930, he had the greatest confidence-he has changed his mind somewhat in the intervening years, as a great many other people in this dominion have done-made the statement that there would be an even greater number employed than the estimate of the Prime Minister would indicate. On page 319 of Hansard of September 17, 1930, he said:
The right hon. gentleman says that the consumers will suffer. I will teli him and those around' him what will happen. When these measures, which are now in existence, if they are not defeated-and they certainly will not be-are in full effect, they will provide work for some 30,000 to 50,000 industrialists in this country.
How far this estimate of the ex-Minister of Trade and Commerce was justified can be judged by the figures which I will subsequently submit. It is now common knowledge, I think, that the changes which were made in the tariff in 1930, again in 1931 and in subsequent years, aggravated if they did not create the sweatshop labour conditions which we have recently witnessed. We find in the speech from the throne in 1931 that these words are put into his excellency's mouth:
My government has explored the origins of our difficulties and is firmly of the belief that many of our problems do not arise out of world wide depression, but are antecedent to it; and that domestic factors have also largely determined the degree of economic distress from which this country is suffering.
What were the antecedent conditions we find indicated by the next paragraph in which, true to Conservative policy, it is stated that what needed changing was the tariff; and we were assured that the changes brought about in 1930 and those that would be introduced in 1931 would be the cure-all for the evils from which the country was suffering. In the session of 1932, which opened on February 4, we find this statement:

The provisions made at the last session of parliament for unemployment and farm relief are proving effective.
Proving effective? Why, just three months prior to that the late Senator Gideon Robertson, at that time Minister of Labour, had given out the statement that in September, 1931, there were 530,000 out of work in Canada. In fairness one should point out that it was also stated at that time that of the 530,000, some 150,000 were agriculturists in the west, but even at that we have to start the winter of 1931 with the startling figure of some
400,000	souls in Canada out of work. During the winter of 1931-32 there was put into operation a public works program in cooperation with the municipalities and the provinces. That this government recognized late in 1931 that this was a national problem is borne out by the fact that the order in council passed after the first unemployment relief act stated as follows:"]

1182	COMMONS
Unemployment Relief-Mr. Mackenzie
It is true, Mr. Speaker, that during the present session this house has been considering important measures of social reform, and I think it only fair and just to say that in the consideration of these reform measures there has been evinced a most commendable degree of cooperation by all sections of the house. At this time I am not permitted to discuss the measure of unemployment insurance which the house has been discussing both on second reading and in committee of che whole; neither am I permitted by the rules of the house to discuss in detail the legislation with regard to the eight hour day, that concerning minimum wages or the legislation concerning the general situation with regard to wages and hours. But I think I am permitted under the rules to say-and I think this was admitted by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) himself only the other day-that the measures of reform we have had before us so far, and the measures of reform which have been brought to our attention by means of resolutions placed on the order paper, do not touch this vital, challenging problem of unemployment relief as we have that problem in Canada at the present time.
I should like to quote some figures, which I am sure will startle every hon. member of this house. This afternoon in response to a question which I had the honour to ask the administration opposite, I received some statistics dealing with the unemployment relief situation as it exists, practically at the present moment, throughout Canada. I intend to give the figures to the house, though I am sure it is not necessary in order that the house may be seized of the tremendous importance of this problem. The reply of the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs (Mr. Murphy) was that there were 23,187 on relief under the jurisdiction of that department. The reply from the Department of Pensions and National Health indicated that there were in receipt of relief administered by that department-which I may say is a great and merciful work, because it renders valuable assistance to pensioners and their dependents throughout the dominion, and at the present time I am only endeavouring to emphasize the magnitude of the problem which must be driven home with all possible force to every member of this house-some 8,912 pensioners, 6,684 wives of pensioners and 15,858 children. Then I come to the last department, the Department of Labour, and I find that at the present time there are on direct relief under the administration of that department 235,467 heads of families and

832,931 dependents of such heads of families, in addition to 38,927 individual relief cases covering one person only. That makes a total of 1,107,325 persons receiving direct relief under the Department of Labour, and if we add the number receiving other than direct relief the total is swelled to the appalling and astounding figure of 1,207,345. I think, sir, this reply to the question I asked is ample justification for bringing the matter to the attention of the ministry at the present time.
Now I wish to direct the attention of the house to a question I asked the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) on the evening of February 19. When the house was in committee of supply, discussing the labour vote, I asked the minister a question, and in reading it now I am not being critical; I am putting this on the record so that we may have the record clear and may know exactly what is the attitude of the administration with respect to this all important and transcendent national problem. I asked:
Is the Minister of Labour prepared to give any information in regard to his policy this year with reference to the unemployment situation or does he intend to discuss the matter under some other item?
Mr. Gordon: That will be taken up under another item later.
Mr. Mackenzie (Vancouver): Under which item of the estimates? We are passing now the labour vote, No. 14.
Mr. Gordon: Yes, civil government.
Mr. Mackenzie (Vancouver): Under which item shall we have an opportunity of discussing the government policy with respect to unemployment relief?
Mr. Gordon: With respect to unemployment relief, the whole problem is under consideration by the government and has been and is constantly under consideration, and is more likely to be brought before parliament in the form of specific legislation than by w'ay of items in the supply of the labour department.
Then my hon. friend from West Middlesex (Mr. Elliott) asked this further question:
When is the unemployment policy likely to come before the house? A good many hon. members are very anxious to know *what it is and when we may expect it.
The Minister of Labour replied:
The policy or plan of immediate relief will be largely determined by the position in which the provinces find themselves and' by the representations that they may make to the dominion government for help. Upon their representations will largely depend the course of the government with respect to assistance to them. With regard to works that are purely federal, the plans are under consideration by the government and are not yet in such shape that they can be submitted to the house.

Unemployment Relief-Mr. Mackenzie
Again, in reply to a further question, the minister said:
When that is made apparent, then I assume, if the dominion has to come to the aid of the provinces again for the coming year, appropriate legislation will, if it is found necessary, be submitted to the house for discussion and approval.
I asked a further question:
Do I understand the minister to suggest that the policy of this government is to be based entirely on the nature of the requests received from the various provincial governments in regard to the next fiscal year?
The answer was:
Largely, yes.
So, Mr. Speaker, I think I am justified in stating to the house at this time that the policy of the administration in regard to this all important question of national unemployment relief is a policy of waiting until they receive certain indefinite requests from the various provinces. As a government charged with the tremendous, comprehensive responsibility of administering the affairs of this dominion, at the present moment they have no policy whatever in dealing with these
1,207,000	people throughout the dominion who are on relief. As I mentioned before they admit it, using as their mouthpiece the Minister of Labour who is charged with the responsibility of administering this department.
During the course of the debate on the unemployment insurance bill the Prime Minister said he had some plans and some policies with respect to unemployment relief. This was in the nature of an obiter dictum, an aside, with respect to the question of unemployment insurance. All parties are here, all members of this House of Commons, in a humble endeavour and desire to assist our constituents and to assist in the general interests of the Dominion of Canada. If the Prime Minister has a plan or policy for dealing with this tremendous problem of unemployment, why does he not frankly promulgate it so that hon. members may discuss it? My personal view is that this is a matter which compels and challenges our attention The advocacy of the Liberal party in connection with this problem is that we are prepared to shelve the consideration of all other matters already before parliament or to be brought before parliament, and to discuss immediately this tremendous and emergent problem of unemployment.
In the time at my disposal I desire to discuss the matter from two viewpoints, first from the viewpoint of the policies which have been pursued by the administration opposite since the year 1930, and in the second place, if I
may be permitted, from a constructive viewpoint I shall endeavour to deal with the magnitude and severity of our most compelling national problem.
The most astounding fact I have ever noted during my experience in this chamber is that in the very actuarial report submitted by the government opposite and written by the man who was their technical expert in connection with the preparation of the unemployment insurance bill now before this House of Commons there is the most scathing condemnation I have ever read of this administration and its policy since 1930. First I should like to read from a book written by the same gentleman, Mr. Hugh H. Wolfenden, entitled The Real Meaning of Social Insurance. Under the heading Trade Restrictions at pages 109 and 110 I find the following:
Under this heading, as contributory if not primary causes of unemployment, particularly in exporting countries, may be listed tariffs, immigration restrictions and other impediments to the free interchange of goods and workers. Probably more than in the case of any other cause of unemployment are these factors possible of amelioration only through the actions of enlightened statesmen.
Then I read, from the actuarial report, tables, if you please, Mr. Speaker, presented by the Prime Minister himself only a few days ago, said to be the actuarial basis for the legislation he gave us and submitted for the approval of the house and the country. Here is what the same actuarial expert states, Mr. Hugh H. Wolfenden, at page 10, paragraph 24:
There can be little doubt that the unprecedented rate of unemployment recently experienced is attributable largely to international impediments to the free and natural interchange of goods, services and workers by means of tariffs, quotas, embargoes, special duties, nationalistic legislation, subsidies, manipulation of exchange rates, and migration obstacles, and that the situation is being aggravated by the increasing tendencies within each country to abandon the doctrine of caveat emptor to proscribe selling prices (and so create artificial rather than free markets). to proscribe natural correctives, and to regulate earnings, prices, hours, production and markets and so render them unnatural and inflexible. These innumerable artificial devices have resulted in the v-idespread obstruction of distribution and exchange; they have produced in many countries an appearance of overproduction and in others a state of want which is still unrelieved; and it is now frequently suggested that this situation should be dealt with by restricting production as well as distribution, rather than by freeing the channels of distribution and thus encouraging exchange and trade.
That is indeed a most complete history of Toryism in Canada since 1930. May I just for a few moments recapitulate under the

speechtext: It is a House of Commons speech, giving a record of your maladministration. It would be advisable for all of us to maintain our good humour, because the record will go on in any case.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The old order has gone; the old man will go.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Who has offered the greatest impediment to the free and natural exchange of goods and services? Who has been one of the greatest sinners in world politics? The Conservative party of Canada, under the narrow self-centred nationalistic policy of "Canada first," have led the march of the world for higher tariffs. Let me just quote-

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Pretty fair.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Not like the indifferent, nasal, inaudible remarks of the Minister of Marine. What has the Conservative party done by means of party legislation? They are a marvellous example of an administration which has set up the most artificial barricades in the history of the Dominion of Canada. They have raised ramparts of ruin all around our Canadian land. Yes, they have set the greatest example of tariff raising in our history. I have seen an article valued at $183 which was charged tariffs and excise taxes amounting to $141, or 77i per cent. I have seen invoices of cheaper suitings carrying tariff charges of 87 per cent. I have seen invoices of silk from Great Britain carrying tariff charges of 73 per cent. I have seen invoices for blankets with charges of 50 per cent; silks from France with charges of 66 per cent, and silks from Japan with charges of 244 per cent. All this has happened in the past four and a half years.
Now we come to quotas. One of the bad features about this administration has been the quota system. Under the empire agreements our exportations are to a great extent regulated by quotas existing on some products in the British Isles. Then what about embargoes? I wonder how many hon. members remember the holy days of 1930 and 1931 when the Prime Minister rose in righteous wrath and indignation and condemned that ungodly country known as Russia. In sympathy he placed embargoes on certain articles of importation from Russia. Now, in an excess of oleaginous hypocrisy, he allows certain goods to be imported from Russia and

he even supports-this great enthusiast of 1931-he even supports the entry of unholy Russia to the league of nations. As a matter of fact, I believe she takes our seat on the international labour conference.
And subsidies, Mr. Speaker, the bonusing of wheat and other iniquitous policies of the kind, were promulgated and pursued by this administration. Subsidies on wheat were largely withdrawn. Then, there was the manipulation of exchange rates. Yes, we remember the dumping duty against the British pound. Then, after promoting a system of bonusing wheat production this government the next year, with its customary inconsistency, enforced not a bonus but a restriction on the acreage of wheat in Canada.
With regard to all these policies so strongly condemned by Mr. Wolfenden in his memorable pamphlet, the Prime Minister of Canada and the then Tory party-heaven only knows what it could be called now-sowed the wind and the Canadian nation is now reaping the whirlwind.
Let us lay the basis clearly and concisely by referring to the promises made. I hope I am not transgressing the rules of the house which forbid useless or vain reiteration in debate. Undoubtedly these promises have on many occasions been placed on Hansard. But they are so remarkable, Mr. Speaker, so all embracing, so comprehensive, they illustrate so splendidly what the Prime Minister promised to the Dominion of Canada, that I think I might be permitted to place upon the record once more just a meagre percentage of those promises so that the house can recall the fact that in 1930 the present Prime Minister made most definite and emphatic declarations with regard to his unemployment policy. Speaking in Calgary in June, 1930, he said:
I will not permit this country with my voice or vote to ever become committed to the dole system. I will not permit those to share in any benefit unless they are willing to work and my duty is to provide work to do.
No doles in 1930, but in this year of our Lord, 1935, 1207,000 on the dolel In the same campaign, later on the Prime Minister said:
It must be remembered that promises with respect to policies are matters of profound importance to the Canadian pepole, and the policies we promised to put into effect we propose to put into effect immediately.
At Edmonton, another splendid city of the west, in June, 1930, he said this:
I say again that I will call parliament together at the earliest possible moment to provide at once the remedy-employment for all who can and will work.

Unemployment Reliej-Mr. Mackenzie
At Victoria, the beautiful capital of the most beautiful province of Canada, British Columbia, speaking on June 17, 1930, he said:
Is there any excuse for Canada to have hard times if the government is discharging its duties as it should?
If that statement was appropriate in 1930, with 100,000 unemployed in Canada at that time, I ask this house is it not equally true in 1935 when we have over 600,000 unemployed, with unemployment increased sixfold after an expenditure, including all government agencies of public operations, of over $400,000,000 to meet the terrible challenge of that situation? In Calgary, his own city, in June, 1930, the Prime Minister said:
But this is a new country and there is no excuse for unemployment in Canada if a government does its duty.
In Calgary again:
This problem has ceased to be local but has become national in its importance.
In Montreal during the same election:
Unemployment has become a national problem in Canada.
I want hon. members to remember that word "national," because in 1932 he went once again to Calgary and there we witnessed a most tremendous conversion, almost as remarkable as the conversion we witnessed in the Prime Minister's radio broadcasts last January. It has been said by a great Canadian that Saul was converted on the way to Damascus and Bennett was converted on the way to defeat.
Let me very briefly give the record of the Tory measures commencing with the special session which met here on September 8, 1930. Speaking on September 9, 1930, the Prime Minister said-and this was after we had met in this house, after he had been elected and after we were here in opposition:
It must be remembered that promises with respect to policies are matters of profound importance to the Canadian people, and the policies we promised to put into effect we propose to put into effect immediately.
Not in 1931, not in 1932, not in 1933 or 1934 or 1935, but "immediately," and that was the Prime Minister's promise made on the floor of this house on the second day after the house met in the special session of 1930. Again, at page 39 of Hansard of that special session, the Prime Minister said this:
I shall content myself with saying to the right hon. leader of the opposition and his friends that we will keep the promises we made.
Then again, introducing his resolution on unemployment in this house on September 10, he said:
We do believe that this resolution which I am now submitting ... combined with the measures which will be subsequently submitted-
And what were those measures? Raising the tariff on over two hundred articles, and mostly against the motherland, on the eve of the imperial economic conference of 1930.
We do believe that this resolution which I am now submitting ... combined with the measures which will be subsequently submitted to this house ... will go far to relieve the situation.
Again:
It will be observed that the present number-
He was speaking of the number of the unemployed:
-is something over 117,000, and it is believed that that number will approximate 177,000 during the winter.
It will be within the recollection of the house that at that special session a bill was introduced and passed voting $20,000,000 for works and undertakings of a supposedly useful nature under the supervision of the federal government. I want to lay down four observations made from this side of the house at that time so that I can prove that from session to session there has been a complete consistency in the attitude which we took on all the unemployment measures since 1930.
We asked in the first place for a national audit by the auditor general of the funds expended; second, for detailed estimates of the expenditures to be laid before the house; third, for the appropriate procedure by the committee of supply; fourth, for a national relief commission, representing all the great interests in the state, to administer the whole system of unemployment relief in the Dominion of Canada.
I come now to the regular session of 1931, and I look at the words contained in the speech from the throne in that year. The Prime Minister put these words into the mouth of His Excellency:
The operation of the Unemployment Relief Act of 1930 has proved equally beneficial.
Then, sir, during the session of 1931 we witnessed repeated and emphatic requests from all the opposition, from members to my far left and from ourselves, that the government deal with this question of unemployment, and I wish to place on Hansard once again what took place. Three days before the session prorogued, on July 29,
1186	COMMONS
Unemployment Relief-Mr. Mackenzie
1931, the Prime Minister took up the last government order upon the order paper for 1931, and moved this resolution:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to confer certain powers upon the governor in council in respect to unemployment and farm relief; and for the maintenance of peace, order and good government in all parts of Canada; and to authorize the governor in council to expend for the said purposes out of the consolidated revenue fund such sums as may from time to time be necessary.
May I recapitulate what took place during that session? On March 20 the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) asked the Minister of Labour if any special measures were contemplated to cope with the unemployment situation. The Prime Minister refused to answer that question. On March 23 the then member for Kenora-Rainy River, Hon. Peter Heenan, asked what the government intended to do with respect to the relief of unemployment. The Prime Minister said:
The question can stand.
On March 31 the hon. member for North Winnipeg moved the adjournment of the house to discuss a matter of urgent public importance, namely, the acute distress arising from unemployment.
I am just reminded, Mr. Speaker, that according to the rule I have only ten minutes left, and I shall therefore give notice of my amendment so that I shall be quite in order. I intend to move the following amendment:
That all the words after the word "That" in the motion be struck out, and the following substituted therefor:
This house regrets that, notwithstanding the specific promises made prior to the election of 1930. and many times since reiterated, and despite the fact that extraordinary powers to deal with unemployment have been repeatedly secured from parliament, the present administration, after nearly five years of office, has not yet submitted to parliament any definite or effective policy to deal with widespread actual unemployment or distress which continues to be Canada's most urgent national problem.
I proceed now with the record. The hon. member for North Winnipeg on March 31, as I say, moved the adjournment of the house to discuss a matter of urgent public importance, namely the acute distress arising from unemployment. After a lengthy discussion the motion was ruled out of order.
On April 17 the then member for Kenora-Rainy River, Hon. Peter Heenan, brought up the question again, and failing to get an answer moved the adjournment of the house. That motion was defeated by a vote 82 to 56. On April 24 the hon. member for Bow River

(Mr. Garland) asked whether the government intended to call a dominion unemployment conference, and the Prime Minister answered:
The hon. member will be advised when the event happens, if it does happen.
On May 25 the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (M. Neill) brought to the attention of the Minister of Labour the desperate unemployment situation prevailing in the city of Nanaimo. The Minister of Labour said the question was purely provincial. On May 26, on a motion to go into supply, the house discussed the urgent necessity of holding a conference with the provinces. No member of the government took part in that debate. On June 16 the leader of the opposition, in the budget debate, urged a conference with the provinces to deal with unemployment. No attention whatever was paid by the government to that suggestion. On June 29 Hon. Peter Heenan asked for a statement of government policy on unemployment, and the Prime Minister replied:
At an appropriate time a statement will be made. The primary duty with respect to unemployment does not rest with the federal government.
On June 30 after three or four days' discussion, the hon. member for Willow Bunch (Mr. Donnelly) directed attention to the appalling conditions prevailing in rural Saskatchewan, and the Prime Minister said:
The primary responsibility rests with the municipalities and with the provinces.
On July 9 the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) asked when the government would introduce legislation on unemployment, and the Prime Minister said that legislation would be introduced when the business of the house had been practically disposed of. That resolution, moved by the Prime Minister on behalf of the government three days before parliament was prorogued in 1931, consisted of three parts: In the first place, that it was expedient to bring in a measure to confer certain powers on the governor in council in respect of unemployment relief; second, some measures with respect to farm relief; and third, a measure to confer certain powers on the governor in council for the maintenance of peace, order and good government throughout the dominion. Our position in regard to this matter was made abundantly clear. We proposed in the first place that he should ask the house to vote a certain sum for unemployment relief, a certain sum for farm relief, and to indicate what he thought necessary for the preservation of peace, order and good government in Canada. We refused at that time, as

Unemployment Relief-Mr. Mackenzie
we have done every session since, to surrender the rights of parliament with respect to control over expenditures; we would not dispense at one fell swoop with the entire authority of this house and give to the government a blanket authority to deal with this trinity of measures which I have mentioned, namely, the unemployment situation, the farm relief situation and the preservation of peace, order and good government in the dominion.
That brings me to the first session of 1932, opened on February 4 of that year. The speech from the throne contained these words:
Conditions are gradually improving-
They were still improving in 1932.
This period of trial has shown the Canadian situation to be fundamentaly sound.
We moved an amendment on going into supply on February 23, 1932. It was moved by Mr. Heenan that the measures introduced by the government were inadequate and ineffective to deal with unemployment. By that time it had become quite manifest that the legislation of 1931 was a complete and dismal failure, and while debate was in progress the following resolution appeared on the order paper:
Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a bill to amend chapter 58 of the statutes of Canada, 1931, striking out the word "March" and substituting the word "May" therefor.
This was much worse than the legislation of 1931. I want to make it clear to the members of this house that whereas the peace, order and good government provisions were contained in the legislation of 1931, they were only suggested by the administration to come into effect after parliament had risen and the members had gone home. But when they introduced the legislation of 1932, when they attempted to revive the dead statute embodied in that resolution, they asked for complete authority and jurisdiction to deal with all questions involving peace, order and good government, while this parliament was sitting and while the members of this house were seated supinely here, not knowing what the cabinet council were doing with respect to peace, order and good government. That I characterize as the most audacious, the most amazing, the most barefaced piece of legislation introduced by the Prime Minister in a free parliament. It was a complete, a pro-'ound and a convincing demonstration of the impotence, the incompetence and the incapacity of the administration to deal with this great question of unemployment in the dominion.
And now we come to the legislation of March 8, 1932. We again stated our position 92582-76
in clear and unmistakable terms. We expressed our willingness to vote the sums necessary, and in committee we made our position once more abundantly clear. We objected to the powers of parliament and the resources of the treasury being handed over to the keeping of any cabinet in the dominion. It was a virtual dictatorship, despotism of the rankest kind set up in Canada. Let me now remind the house what was done under these despotic powers which this cabinet assumed under the authority of peace, order and good government.
First, the government prohibited the exportation of gold except under licence and by the chartered banks. That was October 19, 1931. In the second place, on new year's eve, December 31, the government in a great hurry put through another order in council enabling the life insurance companies in Canada to place a false valuation on their investments; they were enabled to take the valuation of June 30, 1931 instead of December 31, 1931. Thirdly, on October 27, 1931 there was passed an order in council, P.C. 2693, which virtually amended the Bank Act, authorizing the banks to make all government returns with regard to securities in a way other than that prescribed by the Bank Act. In other respects the procedure for amending the Bank Act is clearly laid down and any amendments are considered by a committee of this house every ten years; but this cabinet, this cabal, amended the Bank Act by this order in council, making a revaluation of banking securities. In the fourth place, on December 16 an order in council was passed, P.C. 3087, on the recommendation of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) increasing the strength of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police by 300 men, with an added expenditure of $274,135. The government increased the armed forces of the crown, even though they were a police force, without a single reference to the authority of parliament. Never had there been such a flouting of the supremacy of parliament as took place in that order in council increasing the numbers of the mounted police by 300 and imposing on the taxpayers of the country, without consulting parliament, an additional obligation of $274,000.
On September 12, 1931, the government passed order in council P.C. 2238, guaranteeing repayment to the chartered banks of amounts of money advanced the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers Limited, and this house and the country do not yet know to what extent the taxpayers of Canada are obligated by this venture in gambling, which was authorized, subsidized and supported by the government. Again, there was another guarantee

1188	COMMONS
Unemployment Relief-Mr. Mackenzie
of 160,000,000 to the Canadian Pacific Railway and, if you please, during the session of 1933, while this house was actually sitting, these secret negotiations went on between the banks of this dominion and the government. And we were never apprised of one single iota of the negotiations. Worse than that, three days before parliament prorogued, a letter was written by the Prime Minister guaranteeing $60,000,000 of the taxpayers' money to support a private corporation. In the committee on banking and commerce a year ago, as will be found in the sworn evidence which appears in the bluebooks, we asked the general manager of the Bank of Montreal whether that bank would have renewed a loan of $20,000,000 for another year, and the answer was in the affirmative. We asked the same gentlemen whether the other banks of Canada would have looked after the remaining $17,519,000 odd for the period of another year, the money which this corporation required to take care of its immediate obligations, and the answer was again in the affirmative. There was therefore no immediate financial necessity for the guarantee, and yet this government, without consulting parliament, without consulting a single member guaranteed $60,000,000 of the people's money to the Canadian Pacific Railway under the guise of unemployment relief, while hundreds of thousands of people were on the verge of starvation throughout the dominion and the municipalities and provinces were nearing bankruptcy.
I come now to the second session of 1932. We met on October 6 of that year and the speech from the throne contained the following :
The problem of unemployment continues to receive the anxious attention of my ministers. Under the powers granted them at the last session of parliament, they have been able to develop further, in cooperation with the provinces and municipalities, a scheme of direct relief to be put into operation during the autumn and winter months to the extent required by prevailing conditions. Plans for the reestablishment of the unemployed in various parts of the country are in preparation and will become operative as soon as, in the opinion of my ministers, the public expenditure incident thereto will be productive of commensurate benefits.
This was a complete abandonment of the policies theretofore pursued, and an open avowal of the dole system by way of unemployment relief. "Plans for the reestablishment of the unemployed"-what did that mean? In the light of subsequent events, it meant absolutely nothing.
Then the Prime Minister went to Calgary, his own constituency, and he spoke there on

September 6 of the same year. Let us recall the promises. He said repeatedly in 1930 that this was no longer a local or provincial question; that it was a national one. Listen to what he said in Calgary on September 6, 1932:
So far as I am concerned the administration of relief does not lie with the dominion government. I am not prepared to scrap the constitution-
What a remarkable change between 1932 and 1935!
-and say the primary responsibility can be shifted to the dominion government.
I have not yet reached the point where I think the dominion government is better equipped to deal with these matters than either the provinces or the municipalities.
The problem was national in 1930! It was provincial and local in 1932. The Canadian Pacific had received their guarantee of $60,000,000.
I now come to November 21, 1932, when the hon. member for North Winnipeg asked for a committee or commission to study this question, stating that at that time the number of unemployed was 750,000. The only encouragement he received was to be ruled out of order.
On the house meeting again after the Christmas recess on February 22, 1933, the Minister of Labour, whose legislation was expiring on March 31, introduced the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to continue in force the provisions of the Relief Act, 1932, until the 31st of March, 1934.
In other words, the only policy of this administration was one of repeating and repeating the same old legislation from year to year. In the first place public works were mixed up with relief; then there was the straight dole, and now one year continuing the doleful legislation of another. On March 3, 1933, a further amendment was moved by one of the ministers after the resolution was in committee, as follows:
Provided, however, that the amount to be paid for direct relief for the fiscal year ending the 31st of March, 1934, shall not exceed the sum of $20,000,000.
During the debate we discovered that the amount expended under the 1930 legislation was $17,987,000; on public works, around $14,000,000, and in direct relief, about $3,500,000. Under the legislation of 1931 and 1932 the dominion government had subscribed the sum of $41,000,000. Then the government, still wobbling, pursuing with faltering footsteps their erratic course, had to move even a second
FEBRUARY 25, 1935	11S9
Unemployment Reliej-Mr. Mackenzie
amendment to their own resolution in committee. The Minister of Railways (Mr. Man-ion) on March 20, 1933, moved:
And that provision be made for accepting securities from the provinces for such loans, advances, guarantees, etc., as may be advanced by the government, and that provision also be made for the maintenance of peace, order and good government throughout Canada.
In other words, the clause with respect to peace, order and good government which, after the opposition by those on this side of the house, had been abandoned by the administration in the previous year, was reinserted in the legislation of 1933 on a resolution moved by the Minister of Railways on March 23 of that year.
May I be pardoned by the house for quoting some of the observations I made in that debate? Speaking on this resolution on March 20, 1933, I said:
Considering the emergent conditions that prevail in many of our Canadian cities, surely the time has arrived for the government of the day, in a large national and constructive way, to envision and comprehend their entire problem as a nation-wide problem, a Canadian problem, in its very essence, and as far as I personally am concerned, if the government deals with it as a national problem I shall be only too glad to render any assistance I can. It is a national problem, Mr. Chairman, because our municipalities are practically all bankrupt. They are out of resources, and I am afraid that the policies of the administration during the last few years have very largely been driving them to that condition because they have been compelled to live beyond their resources to face the present emergent situation. So I am appealing to the Minister of Labour, particularly in view of the very grave conditions that exist in the province of British Columbia and all through the Canadian west, both in the industrial centres and on many of the farms in western Canada, to deal with this question in a national way, not in any piecemeal fashion, providing one scale of relief nere and anpther there, not with the present lack of coordination and uniformity throughout the dominion; but let us have a large national constructive scheme with federal control and direction of the unemployment situation, and then with cooperation between all parties in this house who want to see real remedies applied and real relief obtained, I believe that we shall be able to do something to meet the unemployment situation in this dominion.
The speech from the throne in 1934 contained only two paragraphs dealing with the situation, as follows:
Improved world conditions-
Improvement every year-improvement in 1930; improving still more in 1931; improving still further in 1933, and then in 1934:
. Improved world conditions are reflected in Canada by expanding trade, improving revenues, and a more confident outlook upon the future.
92582-764	.
My government propose further to promote employment by expenditures on essential public works throughout the dominion.
I wish to mention nine specific points which were emphasized by us at the time in regard to the resolution moved by the Minister of Labour and in regard to the policy pursued by this administration:
1.	A dominion-provincial conference to consider the financial relations of the provinces and the dominion.
2.	That unemployment was Canada's most urgent national problem, and strongly advocated a representative national commission to coordinate all national effort and to cooperate with the provinces and municipalities in the administration of unemployment relief.
3.	That there should be an audit by the federal government of all expenditure of public moneys.
4.	That all moneys for relief purposes should be voted for specific purposes and voted by parliament.
5.	We opposed voting public moneys in lump sums and we opposed the blank cheque -a government policy which subsequently resulted in a colossal wastage of public money.
6.	We opposed giving to the executive the power of legislating by order in council with respect to peace, order and good government
7.	We advocated as the only real basis on which recovery could be hoped for, the introduction of policies which would serve to provide employment by reviving industry and trade and which would make for the liberation of trade both external and internal.
8.	We advocated the development of the basic industries as a way of furnishing employment.
9.	We advocated measures for the control of credits and the democratization of industry.
On February 5, 1934, the hon. member for North Winnipeg moved a further resolution emphasizing the importance of the question of purchasing power, the necessity of a reduction in the hours of labour and the necessity for the more equitable distribution of wealth. That resolution was carried by the house, but no concrete action was taken with respect thereto.
The Minister of Labour on March 22, 1934, moved the following:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure respecting relief measures generally similar in terms to the Relief Act, 1933, but which also makes provision for payment of federal proportion of delayed relief accounts, if any, which may be received subsequent to the date of the expiration of said act.
1190	COMMONS
Unemployment Relief-Mr. Mackenzie
In other words the dole was continued On March 26, 1934, during the debate on the second reading of the bill, very grave irregularities were brought to light as the result of the first report of the auditor general respecting the administration of relief funds in the provinces. We moved an amendment on the third reading of the bill again protesting against taking away from parliament its complete control over public expenditures.
That brings me to the 1935 session. Since then we have had the Prime Minister's broadcasts, and what has happened so far during the present session. May I be permitted to refer in the meantime to just one sentence used by the Prime Minister in his broadcast, when he said, "The world is in tragic circumstances; the signs of recovery are few and doubtful." Yet when I go back and look at the expressions of opinion by hon. ministers since 1930, I find the following. Speaking on October 1, 1930, the Prime Minister said, "that the old order of things had passed.' In western Canada on new year's eve-December 31, 1930-at Regina, he said:
I am satisfied we will he able to look back on the year 1931 with satisfaction

I want you to believe that we are on the highroad to success....
Our minister to Japan is at this hour on his way to China to discuss with the government of that great country the purchase of millions of bushels of our wheat.
Then he came back to Ottawa, and on April 28, 1931, he is reported as having said:
We can look forward to the future with confidence, convinced that the great pathway of peace and prosperity has never appeared so attractive ... so attractive that no words of mine can describe it.

I think there are some evidences that we have reached the dead level of depression and that the movement from now on will be upward.
