I think there are signs of improvement on the horizon, evidences that we have reached the dead level of this depression.

Next year will be the beginning of a new era of prosperity.
Then at sea, on board the Empress of Britain, August 28, 1933:
I trust all may enjoy happiness, opportunity to work as we return to prosperity, and contentment under a kindly providence in this great land we call our home.
And again in Montreal, on September 1, 1933:
In the dominion, particularly, I note that conditions are becoming better.
And my hon. friend the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion), on September 3, 1933, expressed his satisfaction in Canada's leadership. He said:
With our Prime Minister once more at the helm-

after his strenuous efforts in London, we can go forward in confidence that all will soon be well again.

-on September 19, 1933, said:
Some people look and wonder whither we are moving. I have never had the slightest doubt as to where we were going. I am one of those sturdy individualists who believe we are moving upward and onward.
Again in Winnipeg on October 10, 1933:
We may, I think, confidently look forward to better days. Slow, yes, but none the less sure.
And then in Manitoba on the same day:

Unemployment Relief-Mr. Mackenzie
At Montreal on June 8, 1934, from the
Canadian Press:
Expressing his belief that Canada was stand- * ing on the threshold of a prosperity greater than she had ever known, Prime Minister R. B. Bennett told an audience here that at least one out of every twelve Canadian men, women and children were on a payroll on May 1st.
Yet when the time came for the broadcast the right hon. gentleman said the world was in tragic circumstances, although year after year from 1930 until 1935 we had nothing but prosperity around the corner, even in the utterances of my good friend the Minister of Railways.
Now, sir, I come to one or two other paragraphs in these radio addresses which brought such wonderful confidence and satisfaction to my esteemed and venerable friend the Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan):
I promised I would end unemployment. That was a definite undertaking. By it I stand.
This is five years afterwards:
Unemployment in Canada is one of the consequences of the awful and unprecedented depression.
Yet every year from 1930 prosperity was just around the comer. Again he said:
When the system is reformed and in full operation again there will be work for all.
That is much worse than the former promises. In 1930 he said he would end unemployment immediately or perish in the attempt. But now, five years later, he is going to end it-when? When the system is reformed. Something mythical and nebulous and uncertain and vague.
When the system is reformed and in full operation again there will be work for all.
Then again he said:
If a man is able and willing to work but can get no work, provision for his security must be made in a decent way.
I completely agree with that sentiment, but why then is no policy brought down by this administration? He said:
We are to put in a permanent system of sound and scientific insurance against unemployment.
I am in favour of that, but I venture this prediction, that not only will the unemployment insurance legislation do nothing for the unemployed in Canada, but it will be many weary months before it will do anything whatever even for the limited number of the employed who will come under its provisions. So that for the problem which I am discussing to-night this measure is entirely inadequate and useless.
Then the Prime Minister said, " the present Old Age Pensions Act is unscientific and obsolete." Was it so in 1930 when the Prime Minister went all across Canada saying he would nationalize the old age pensions scheme and pay one hundred per cent of the cost, as he said in New Brunswick and all through the maritime provinces? Now after five years of his own administration as a result of further broken promises he finds it unscientific and obsolete. I am proud to say that in regard to old age pensions the Liberal party led the way in England and in Canada. In England under Lloyd George in 1911 -I happened to be in the old land at that time-we pioneered in old age pensions legislation. Again in Canada the Liberal party pioneered in old age pensions, and I am proud to say that my province of British Columbia under the Liberal government of good old John Oliver was the first province of Canada to place government old age pensions in operation.
Then he said, " Health, accident and sickness insurance must be developed in the same way." Again I know that under the rules of order I cannot discuss it in detail, but I refer the house to part IV of the unemployment insurance bill of this year.
I come now to this session and1 the speech from the throne, in which we have these words:
I welcome you at a time when our country stands upon the threshold of a new era of prosperity.
It is the same story year after year. In every year from 1930 right up to 1935; " our country upon the threshold of a new era of prosperity"!-and 1,207,000 people on relief to-day out of a population of 10,500,000. Again:
Employment is increasing. Our trade is expanding. The national revenues are higher. These evidences of recovery attest the wisdom and efficacy of the measures you have taken.
My honoured leader, speaking in the debate on the address on January 21, said as reported at page 59 of Hansard:
Let us therefore, between now and that time, take as first measures those dealing with the problem of unemployment and social reform and give them our undivided attention from day to day so that, working together, we may, if at all possible produce something in the way of a solution. I suggest that to that end this debate be permitted to end very speedily after the Prime Minister and the leader of the third party have spoken, unless there is something controversial in what they say. At any rate, so far as the members of the Liberal opposition are concerned, we are prepared in order to deal with the question of unemployment to end this discussion at once.

Unemployment Relief-Mr. Mackenzie
And on January 28, as reported at page 263 of Hansard, the right hon. leader of the opposition moved the following amendment to the motion to go into supply:
That all the words in the motion after the word "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"This house is of the opinion that the immediate consideration of present conditions of unemployment and the introduction of measures of social and industrial reform should not be delayed or postponed by a consideration of supply in advance of the consideration of government policies with respect to unemployment and the introduction of measures with respect to social and industrial reform."
Again on February 5, on the motion of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) to go into supply, the leader of the opposition moved,
as reported on page 496 of Hansard:
That all the words after the word "that" in the motion be struck out, and the following substituted therefor:
"That this house is of the opinion that when it is moved into committee of supply priority should be given consideration of the estimates of the Department of Labour in order that opportunity may be afforded for an immediate discussion and consideration of conditions of unemployment and distress at present existing in all parts of Canada, and of the measures required to cope therewith."
That amendment was ruled out of order by Your Honour. But I want to put on Hansard another quotation from the address of my right hon. leader on that occasion:
We feel very strongly that any program of social and industrial reform should not be permitted to sidetrack an immediate consideration of present problems in our country.
That is the attitude of the official opposition. It is in that spirit and in furtherance of the remarks contained in the address of my leader on that occasion that I offer the amendment which it is my intention to submit be-for I resume my seat.
Then we come to the questions which we asked of the Minister of Labour the other evening in this house. With these questions I began my survey of what has taken place in this house during the last five years, when the hon. member for West Middlesex (Mr. Elliott) asked questions and I asked questions myself as to what the policy of this administration is. When I asked him in regard to what was the policy of this administration with respect to these 1.207,000 people on relief in Canada to-night, the only reply I received was that the policy would have to await the requests received from the provinces with respect to this great national emergency.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I wish to deal rather briefly with the world aspect of this question, and I should like to place on Hansard one or

two figures with respect to the volume of industrial production in the world, which in 1933 was 12Jt per cent greater than in 1932, while the production of foodstuffs remained the same. In the same period the production of raw materials increased by ten per cent, while the same rate prevailed in 1934. The importance of these figures lies in the fact that in 1933 there were three times as many unemployed as in 1929, but by the summer of 1934 there were only twice as many in all the world while in Canada we had six times as many in 1934 under the policies pursued by the administration opposite. Yet, according to Sir Arthur Salter, one of the world's greatest authorities on this question, in the last issue of the Yale Review, the world figures were only twice as great in 1934 as in 1929. International trade has increased only slightly since 1933, and while we may be coming slowly up the slope we are by no means half way up so far, and I think for many weary months to come we must continue to pursue the toilsome ascent from the depths.
Seen in the large the problem of relief transcends the care of our present relief load. It involves the question of whether to-day's relief cases are to become semi-permanent, and whether their numbers are to be augmented by new recruits who cannot find opportunity for self support. It involves something else, the absorption of our unemployed into the ranks of private industry. If our industrial organization cannot provide a living for these men by giving them jobs then it must support them, and ultimately that cost will come back on industry in taxes. The government may be able to stimulate absorption by an extensive construction program, but I am somewhat in doubt' as to the value of construction programs when they are carried on entirely by governmental agencies. We have to develop a new type of public service for the unemployed ; we may have to organize those whom industry cannot now absorb into production for use units. I am sure my hon. friends in the corner will welcome this suggestion. When ordinary industry cannot absorb labour for ordinary production for profit then the nation may have to step in and take up the gap between the efforts of private enterprise and direct relief for those unemployable, and subsidize industries where the wages would not be such as would compete with private enterprise, in order to do two things, first to afford a decent subsistence, and second to develop work of substantial use to the state which will employ these men.
There are four reasons in the main for this problem, because after all, even with this

Unemployment Relief-Mr. Mackenzie
depression the problem may be a semi-permanent one, in spite of the fact that Canada is a new country. First there are the unemployable, who are not able to render effective service in our industrial order, through misfortunes of their own or misfortunes of the system. They present a 'special problem of their own. Then in our industrial order, with its rapidly changing adjustments, workers may find themselves attached to inefficient or decaying industries, and may have to look for other jobs. Seasonal unemployment adds to this total. Third, the codes of many organizations to-day in Canada, as in other nations, make it almost impossible to provide gainful occupations for many of our youth, and to my mind that is one of the greatest problems. Fourth, business cycles of unemployment are inevitable due to several causes, and plans should be laid in advance for periods of depression.
To combat these factors what can one advocate? In the first place there is unemployment and social insurance, with which we have been wrestling during the present session. Second, to meet unemployment and to look after those who cannot be absorbed by an insurance scheme, other measures must be devised combining useful results with continued subsistence. Third, there are the programs of public construction. To my mind, Mr. Speaker, the main thing is that new employment and new purchasing power can be created by encouraging business enterprise in an expanding production and distribution of goods and services. Business itself must be willing to outlaw those forms of competition which are socially destructive, and it must give due shares to labour, the consumer, to management and to capital. It must be content with business profits and must not search unduly after illusory and unsocial speculative gains. It must be willing to endure that minimum of government control which the general interest requires. In short, shall I say, there must be a new partnership between business and politics in Canada for the sake of the common man. Governments need the assistance of constructive and productive business, and I think business needs the guidance and cooperation of governments, not bludgeoning, not dragooning, not. conscripting, but in a real alliance responsive to the promptings of the social conscience.
May I therefore, Mr. Speaker, summarize the situation in Canada as it exists at the present moment. First, after an expenditure of about $400,000,000 in five years we have some 600,000 unemployed and over 1,000,000
on relief. Second, we have over 20,000 single homeless men in the national defence camps scattered throughout the Dominion of Canada. Third, the amounts expended under the special public works appropriation of 1934 have not materially improved the situation. Fourth, very largely as a result of the burdens imposed upon them by relief legislation, many of our municipalities are actually bankrupt and some of our provincial governments are on the verge of bankruptcy, especially in western Canada. Fifth, with such a situation confronting us, one month before the close of the present fiscal year the government says through its Minister of Labour that it has no policy at present with which to meet the situation.
My hon. friends may ask what I advocate, and in the remainder of what I have to say I wish to make it very clear that I am giving my personal views only, and not necessarily the views of any party or group. First, in addition to a national relief commission representative of all interests to administer relief in Canada, which we have advocated for the last four or five years, I suggest that we should have immediately at our disposal a complete census and registration of those now unemployed, with a view to ascertaining the numbers permanently unemployable, and special measures for their care. Second, I want to advocate the handling of this entire problem as one of national emergency, even if only for a limited time, until this depression is over. Third, I advocate the undertaking by the government of public works on a limited scale in which the greater proportion of the appropriation shall go to labour rather than to supplies or equipment. Fourth, I advocate cooperation with the construction industry and other business for privately directed works and undertakings, their financing to be assisted by the government, which shall be completely reimbursed for any advances made. Fifth, I suggest adequate, immediate and effective measures to increase our domestic and foreign trade. Sixth, I suggest the reduction of rates of interest on all outstanding obligations in the Dominion of Canada. Seventh, I suggest a national conversion scheme reducing the interest on all internal debt to two and a half per cent. Eighth, I advocate immediate negotiations with outside nations where our external bonds are held, for a mutually satisfactory scheme for the reduction of interest on external bonds. Ninth, I suggest the increase of our currenc>
by $430,000,000, which is scientifically justifiable by the appreciation of gold values, tc be used for the reduction of our national debt;

not to be used under any pretence in the financing of temporary schemes by the administration during the current year, but to be used for the reduction of our public debt so that thereafter we may finance at low rates of interest any public works or undertakings that we may desire to carry on. Tenth, I advocate that the national budget be strictly balanced. Eleventh, I suggest a financial conference with the provinces to consider the advisability of establishing a national loan board to coordinate, if possible, the investment activities of governments without commingling their financial responsibilities and to consider the exact and precise financial situation of all governmental agencies in Canada.
My last recommendation is in regard to exservice men. For the permanently unemployable I suggest the extension of the principle of the War Veterans' Allowance Act, reducing the age to fifty-five, if only for a limited period. For the partially unemployable I suggest physical reestablishment for a limited period and land settlement on small holdings. For the employable I advocate the scientific placement of men in industry.
Such then, Mr. Speaker, is the problem and such are some of the suggested remedies. No matter what attention this house has given during this session to the so called reform measures; no matter what attention we have given unemployment insurance; no matter what attention we have given or may give hours of work legislation, I say that we shall be recreant to our trust if during this session we do not take steps to meet this urgent national situation. I say the eight hour day bill will do nothing to lessen unemployment in the Dominion of Canada. You must reduce the total hours of labour in one complete week before you can tackle what is essentially the problem of unemployment. So far as I am concerned I am in favour of reducing the hours of labour substantially below the forty-eight hour week. In certain industries, both from the national and the provincial viewpoint, there must be certain exemptions from the hours of labour brought about by mutual consent of the employers and employees. This provision exists in the legislation in British Columbia, and once again may I say that I believe the British Columbia legislation respecting hours of labour is the best in Canada.
I have reviewed the entire situation from 1930 to 1935. Once again I should like to impress upon the government the necessity for enunciating to this House of Commons without further delay its policy with respect to unemployment, distress and prevailing hardship. In that spirit, seconded by the hon.

member for West Lambton (Mr. Gray) I beg to move the following amendment:
That all the words after the word "That" in the motion be struck out, and the following substituted therefor:
This house regrets that, notwithstanding the specific promises made prior to the election of 1930, and many times since reiterated, and despite the fact that extraordinary powers to deal with unemployment have been repeatedly secured from parliament, the present administration, after nearly five years of office, has not yet submitted to parliament any definite or effective policy to deal with widespread actual unemployment or distress which continues to be Canada's most urgent national problem.
I should like to conclude my observations by quoting the final words of a great book, Industry and Humanity-

Speaker, I appreciate the difficulty that faced the acting Prime Minister (Sir George Perley) when he attempted to reply to the very brilliant speech of my colleague from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie). In view of the fact that his leader, the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) has not announced any definite policy with respect to this important matter of unemployment, and that we have not been able to receive one from the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon), it is not difficult to understand why the acting Prime Minister should simply fall back on what has been the policy of the present government since its inception and say, as the right hon. gentleman did in his closing remarks, that "the question is being considered." I say to you, sir, that it has been considered. I have no doubt that from the very first day this government took office until this hour in the fifth year of their life, and the last I hope, they have been and are still considering this problem. We have no quarrel with the acting Prime Minister when he states that his leader has courage; we agree that he has. But one is reminded of the story of the engineer who, seeing a buffalo bull charging his engine, said " I admire your courage but I cannot admire your judgment." The right hon. gentleman points out to-night the situation that various other countries are facing and points to the fact that Canada has led in this respect. But I would remind him and other hon. members of this house of the fact that in 1930 in reply to members on this side the Prime Minister said that the concern of his party and of the people of Canada was Canada and not the United States or any other country.
I offer no apologies for taking part in this debate. Here we are in 1935 waiting for some definite pronouncement on the part of the government as to how they propose to solve this problem. In 1931 and again in 1932 we were told, as we were told the other night by the Minister of Labour, that the government was waiting to see what the provinces would propose. That might have been all right in 1931 or even in the second session of 1932; but after five years, for the Minister of Labour to come into this house and say that he is waiting to see what the provinces will propose indicates a lack of judgment and of any particular program on the part of the government to solve the problem. In my opinion the time is opportune, indeed it is long overdue, to discuss this problem because during the years this government has been in office it has deliberately delayed the discussion of unemployment relief until the dying days of the
session. This is true of every session. In 1930 they held over our heads the fact that the Prime Minister would not go to the imperial conference unless we rushed the legislation. In 1931 the house began its sittings on March 12 and it was not until July 29, or four days before prorogation, that legislation was introduced in connection with unemployment. In 1931 the act was to expire on March 1, but on March 8 it was extended for two months. In 1933 the Unemployment and Farm Relief Act was introduced on March 21, leaving seven days in which to discuss it. In 1934 the act expired on March 31 and the new act was introduced on March 22, and the house adjourned on March 28 until after Easter, leaving only about four days to discuss the measure, including the time necessary for the Senate to pass it.
I submit therefore that we have a right to bring this matter as forcibly as possibly to the attention of the government in the hope that they will appreciate the problem and take some definite action. I do not wish to weary the house by a repetition of what was promised in connection with unemployment, but it is necessary for one to go back to the election of 1930 in order to bring before the house and the country the steps or lack of steps taken by the government to solve the problem.
On July 10, 1930, speaking at Moncton, the present Prime Minister said:
The Conservative party is going to find work for all who are willing to work, or perish in the attempt. It is going to call parliament at the earliest possible date after July 28 and take such steps as will end this tragic condition of unemployment and bring prosperity to the country ag a whole. . . . Mr. King promises consideration of the problem of unemployment. I promise to end unemployment. Which plan do you like best?
At Victoria on June 17 he said:
We cannot tolerate the dole. Men and women of this country want work, not charity. ... Is there any excuse for Canada to have hard times if the government is discharging its duties as it should?
Then he spoke in Quebec as follows:
There was no necessity for a conference on unemploylment, he continued. The solution was too apparent. "What you want is work," he exclaimed, "not conferences, and you are going to get work." Unless his promises to the People of Canada were kept if elected to office, Mr. Bennett said he wanted Quebec and other members of his party to vote him out of office.

policy of the dominion government, and we are prepared to march forward in cooperation with it. Yet during all these years, as pointed out by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, enormous sums have been spent by this government; as of March 28,	1934,
guarantees of some $96,000,000, loans to the provinces of some $52,000,000, and cash under relief measures amounting to $115,000,000. Having spent these enormous sums I claim that my right hon. leader was correct when he urged even at the very first session that there should be an audit of these various expenditures. One has only to look at the report of the auditor general, not only of last year but of this year, in which he complains that he has been understaffed, that the scope of his examinations has been limited because he has not been given the required assistance, and that large sums of money had been over-contributed by the dominion, as indicated on page 25 of his report. From the report of unemployment commissioner Hereford, we find that he has a staff of only some thirty-five to administer this huge matter, and when one considers that only a few days ago in the course of discussion on

the unemployment insurance measure we heard that there might be a commission with a staff of three or four thousand people, one realizes exactly how little the government have really studied this situation. They are prepared now, and I am not finding any fault with it, to set up an economic council; yet when we urged them repeatedly to set up an unemployment commission they steadfastly refused.
In spite of all that has been said with respect to these figures-and I have shown how they have mounted-what has happened? As the hon. member for Vancouver Centre has shown, in spite of all these things the Prime Minister has been going up and down this country and from one end to the other telling the people of Canada that we are on the road to prosperity. I propose to give only one or two quotations. Speaking at Montreal on May 11, 1931, he said:
I think there are some evidences that we have reached the dead level of depression and that the movement from now on will be upward.
At Ottawa on January 31, 1932, in a new year's message, he said:
In my belief the worst is over. Canada has survived the crisis, and the same spirit and the same strength which have withstood the stress and strain of the past year will carry us over all intervening difficulties into an era of prosperity hitherto unknown.
In December, 1932, at London, he said:
Next year will see the beginning of an era of prosperity.
At Winnipeg on October 10, 1933, he said'
Canada is standing on the threshold of
recovery.
On December 3, 1933, he told an audience at Sherbrooke, Quebec:
There are distinct evidences the catastrophe has ended. The dead rock bottom of the depression has been reached.
Then as late as the summer of 1934 we find him telling a Montreal audience:
I believe we have passed and left behind us the great depression we encountered in 1929
and 1930____ We are standing on the threshold
of a greater progress and a greater prosperity than we have ever known.
All during these years we have been at the dead rock bottom, climbing the hill, turning the corner, weathering the storm, seeing the light, and in all that time the Prime Minister, to whom we looked for leadership in connection with this all important problem, was giving us this bright picture as he saw it. It culminated on January 2 of this year-that is an important date-with the new Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hanson) publishing a full page advertisement entitled Cana-

As the year 1934 passes into history, Canada can look back upon a period of unimpaired progress so definitely sustained that it has brought us to the pathway that leads to a sound, sensible, and stable prosperity. The advance that we, as a country, have made during the past year has demonstrated anew the inherent strength and stability of the dominion. We have seen the faith to which we held so firmly in the darker days abundantly fulfilled-the confidence to which we clung in gloomier years triumphantly vindicated. With clearer skies above us, and firmer ground beneath our feet, we have advanced with unimpaired progress along the road of national reconstruction and economic recuperation.
